title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comment_clean:
I am writing to express my serious concerns about the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) DHS Docket No. ICEB-2XXXXX, regarding F-1 student visas. While I understand the goal of strengthening program integrity, several proposed changes would have a profoundly negative and unintended impact on the academic lives of legitimate international students and on the competitiveness of U.S. higher education.

My primary concern is with the proposed prohibitions on academic progression, specifically:

The ban on F-1 students at the graduate level from changing programs.

The ban on F-1 students changing to a program at a lower or same educational level.

These rules, while perhaps intended to prevent visa fraud, fundamentally misunderstand the nature of graduate education and would eliminate critical, legitimate academic pathways. The ban on changing programs is particularly concerning because it ignores the fluid and often unpredictable nature of doctoral research. A student's project is frequently tied to a specific faculty advisor's research and funding grants. If that advisor leaves the university, loses funding, or changes their research direction, the student's entire academic plan can be jeopardized through no fault of their own. In such situations, the only viable option for the student to continue their education and research is often to switch to a different lab, a different advisor, or a related program within the university. This proposal would trap students in untenable academic situations, potentially forcing them to abandon their studies entirely.

The most significant consequence of these rules is the elimination of the ability for a Ph.D. student to "master out." "Mastering out" is not a loophole; it is an established and vital academic process. Doctoral studies are incredibly demanding, and for a variety of valid reasons—such as a shift in research focus, changing career goals, family emergencies, or the realization that a five-to-seven-year Ph.D. is not the right personal fit—a student may decide not to complete the full doctorate. In these cases, universities award an en route master's degree to recognize the multiple years of graduate-level coursework, research, and teaching that the student has successfully completed.

Under the proposed rule, this option would be eliminated for international students. A student would be forced into a rigid, all-or-nothing choice: complete the full Ph.D. or leave the United States after years of hard work with no degree to show for it. This is unnecessarily punitive and fails to acknowledge the value of the academic work performed.

Furthermore, this inflexibility will make U.S. universities less attractive to top-tier international talent. Prospective students will weigh their options and may choose to study in countries like Canada, the United Kingdom, or Australia, where academic pathways are more accommodating. This will harm the research, innovation, and intellectual diversity that international students bring to American campuses.

The authority to determine a student's academic path should remain with the academic institutions. Designated School Officials (DSOs) are trained professionals who are best positioned to verify a student's academic standing and intentions. The current SEVIS system already provides DHS with significant oversight. Imposing these rigid federal restrictions on academic choices is an overreach that will cause more harm than good.

I urge the Department of Homeland Security to reconsider these specific provisions. Please do not punish legitimate students and undermine American higher education in an attempt to address a problem that can be managed through existing oversight mechanisms.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

DHS already has SEVIS to monitor international students and exchange visitors. Forcing every F and J visa holder to file for Extension of Stay (EOS) creates unnecessary paperwork, increasing USCIS caseloads by millions.

Immigration officers’ time would be diverted from enforcement against genuine threats (fraudulent schools, unauthorized overstays, criminal elements) toward processing routine EOS applications for bona fide students.

International students and scholars contribute over $40 billion annually to the U.S. economy, supporting hundreds of thousands of American jobs in universities, housing, healthcare, retail, and technology sectors.

Introducing bureaucratic barriers and uncertainty will push talented students to Canada, the UK, and Australia, which already compete aggressively for global talent.

U.S. businesses—especially in STEM fields critical to America’s leadership in AI, advanced manufacturing, and energy—rely on this pipeline of talent. This rule risks driving innovation away from the United States.

DHS estimates this rule would impose nearly $400 million in new costs over 10 years. These costs would fall not only on students but also on U.S. universities, businesses, and government agencies, which must dedicate resources to unnecessary paperwork.

I respectfully submit the following comments regarding the proposed rule, particularly 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(A) and (C), which would prohibit F-1 graduate students from changing programs during the course of study or from being admitted through a program at the same educational level. While I understand the Department’s concerns about potential misuse of F-1 status, I believe the proposed language is overly restrictive. I encourage DHS to consider targeted modifications that balance the need for oversight with the realities of graduate education.

1. Allow limited graduate-level transfers

Graduate education (especially PhD study) is unique in that it is closely tied to a student’s faculty advisor, research laboratory, and funding source. If an advisor retires, changes institutions, or loses funding, the student may have no realistic choice but to transfer to another program in order to complete their degree. These circumstances are beyond the student’s control and do not indicate any intent to misuse visa status.

Under the proposed rule, however, such students would be forced either to abandon their academic career in the United States or remain in a program where they cannot complete their research. Both outcomes would be detrimental not only to the student but also to U.S. universities and the broader research community.

Instead of imposing a blanket prohibition, DHS could allow graduate-level transfers but limit them to a reasonable number (for example, 1-2 transfer or 2-3 programs at the same level). This would address potential abuse while providing a necessary safeguard for students facing unavoidable academic disruptions.

2. Require consistency with the original visa program

As an additional safeguard, DHS could require that graduate-level transfers remain consistent with the major or program of study for which the F-1 visa was originally granted. For example, if a student entered the United States with an I-20 for a STEM program, any subsequent transfer should also be into a STEM program, rather than into an unrelated discipline.

This requirement would ensure that the student’s academic pathway remains aligned with the purpose for which the visa was issued, while still preserving flexibility within the same general field. Such a measure would address concerns about students using transfers to circumvent visa screening, without imposing an absolute ban that harms legitimate academic progress.

3. Permit re-entry to initiate a new F-1 record

At minimum, graduate students who have legitimate reasons to pursue a second same-level degree or to transfer into another program at the same level should be allowed to do so by departing the United States and re-entering with a new SEVIS record and I-20. This mechanism would apply not only to students seeking a second master’s or PhD, but also to those who must transfer mid-degree due to advisor departure, loss of funding, or a change in academic direction.

Requiring re-entry ensures that each case undergoes an additional layer of scrutiny by U.S. consular officers or CBP at ports of entry. This provides DHS with the security and fraud-prevention safeguards the rule is designed to achieve, while still allowing genuine students the academic flexibility they need. In effect, this approach prevents misuse without imposing an absolute ban that harms legitimate academic progress.

4. Maintain safeguards without harming U.S. competitiveness

International graduate students make substantial contributions to U.S. research and innovation, particularly in STEM fields. Restricting their ability to change programs or pursue additional degrees at the same level risks driving talented individuals to other countries, undermining U.S. global competitiveness.

The existing system already includes strong safeguards: SEVIS monitoring, DSO oversight, and consular/CBP review at the time of visa issuance or re-entry. Rather than an outright prohibition, DHS should build on these tools to prevent abuse while continuing to attract and retain the world’s top academic talent.

For the reasons above, I respectfully urge DHS to revise the proposed provisions to allow limited graduate-level transfers, potentially conditioned on program similarity, and at the very least, to permit students to pursue same-level changes through re-entry under a new SEVIS record. Such modifications would strike a better balance between preventing abuse and maintaining the United States’ reputation as a leader in global education and research.

Thank you for considering my comment. I appreciate the opportunity to provide input during this rulemaking process.

Respectfully

Introduction
I am a foreign student studying at the intersection of biomedical science and business management. I have navigated cross-disciplinary academic experiences during college and plan to continue this trajectory in higher-level education. My perspective reflects both scientific training and practical interest in how education translates into patient impact and economic value.

Background
This comment addresses the NPRM provisions that would (i) restrict changes in educational objectives and school transfers (including within the first academic year and for graduate students) and (ii) bar an F-1 student who has completed a program at one educational level from beginning another program at the same or a lower educational level. See the preamble discussion under “Changes in Educational Objectives” and proposed 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(A)–(E), including § 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(C).

Analysis

The “higher-only” rule conflicts with how modern expertise is built.
The proposal assumes a one-way, hierarchical progression and treats lateral or lower-level study after completion as suspect. The preamble explicitly states that DHS views movement at the same or a lower level as raising bona fides concerns.
In practice, contemporary learning is often modular: professionals deepen targeted competencies via focused master’s or certificates that complement “terminal” degrees. In biomedicine, a physician (M.D.) may pursue a one-year Master of Medical Sciences in Immunology to improve translational trial design. Under the proposal, that coherent, high-value pathway would be categorically blocked solely because the credential is not “higher,” despite its clear professional objective.

Cross-disciplinary training—which the U.S. relies on—would be chilled.
Innovation happens at seams: law + biotech (regulatory and IP), computer science + radiology (AI diagnostics), statistics + epidemiology (trial design), so on and so forth. The proposed bar would steer a J.D. graduate away from a practice-oriented biotechnology master’s (a same-level credential that builds relevant industry understanding) and toward a nominally “higher” degree they may not be prepared for or do not need. The NPRM also proposes to restrict transfers and changes of educational objectives within the first academic year and to constrain graduate-level changes, further narrowing legitimate pathways that universities and employers value.

The fraud-prevention rationale is overbroad and not narrowly tailored.
The preamble cites instances of serial program-hopping, including long tenures in F-1 status. But a blanket prohibition on all same-level or lower-level post-completion study sweeps in many bona fide cases (e.g., clinicians upskilling in biostatistics or regulatory science; scientists adding clinical research management). DHS already proposes other integrity tools—fixed admission periods, extensions of stay (with biometrics), and SEVIS oversight—to address outliers without eliminating legitimate academic progression.

Public-interest harms: patient care, research translation, and competitiveness.
During and after the pandemic, fields like immunology, bioinformatics, and regulatory science became essential to clinical practice. Preventing clinicians and scientists from pursuing targeted, lateral training slows bedside translation and weakens cross-functional literacy on care teams. The U.S. attracts global talent because it enables modular, interdisciplinary study across world-class programs; this rule would push that talent to competitor countries.

Recommendations

Withdraw the provisions that (a) prohibit F-1 students who have completed a program from beginning another program at the same or lower educational level (proposed § 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(C)) and (b) rigidly restrict changes in educational objectives and transfers (including early transfers and graduate-level changes). These sections are detrimental to foreign academic personnel and to the broader U.S. innovation ecosystem.

If DHS retains a control mechanism, replace the categorical bar with a narrowly tailored, case-by-case standard: allow same-level or lower-level programs post-completion when a student shows (i) a coherent professional objective, (ii) program quality/accreditation. Limit approvals to time-bounded programs with normal progress reported in SEVIS; deny where evidence shows serial, unjustified program-hopping.

Conclusion
The proposed “higher-only” pathway and related transfer/objective restrictions are misaligned with how modern expertise is formed, particularly in interdisciplinary domains like biomedicine, and risk unnecessary harm to students, universities, patients, and U.S. competitiveness. DHS should withdraw these provisions, or at minimum replace them with a targeted, evidence-based approach that addresses abuse without stifling legitimate, high-value education.

Legal concerns under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).

XXXXX and DHS v. Regents). Here, the notice does not show that D/S, backed by SEVIS and school reporting, is failing in a way that justifies the broad shift to fixed I-94s. First, contrary to DHS’s claim that international students “consume taxpayer resources,” they are in fact net contributors to the U.S. economy. According to NAFSA (2024), in the 2022–2023 academic year, more than 1.1 million international students contributed $43.8 billion to the U.S. economy and supported over 378,000 jobs. On average, every three international students sustain one U.S. job—not by directly hiring anyone, but through spending on tuition, housing, food, transportation, and services that circulate into universities and communities. I am writing to provide comments on the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM), Establishing a Fixed Time Period of Admission and an Extension of XXXXX for Nonimmigrant Academic Students, XXXXX, and Representatives of Foreign Information Media (Federal Register, XXXXX. 90, No. 165, Aug. 28, 2025). While I understand the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) intent to enhance oversight and national security, I respectfully submit that several provisions—particularly as applied to F-1 academic students—pose significant and unnecessary burdens on international education and the U.S. higher education system.

Many doctoral programs in the United States, particularly in STEM fields, require five to seven years to complete. Imposing a maximum four-year admission period will force nearly all PhD students to apply for one or more Extensions of Stay (EOS). Graduate advisors and institutions cannot easily plan projects when students’ immigration status may be subject to unpredictable processing timelines.

Recommendation: XXXXX and other long-term academic programs to be admitted for the normal duration of the program as indicated on Form I-20, without an arbitrary four-year cap, provided the student continues to make normal academic progress.

2. Restrictions on Educational Pathways (OPT → Graduate Programs)

The proposed rule prohibits F-1 students at the graduate level from changing programs during study and bars students from beginning a new program at the same or a lower educational level. This is unnecessarily restrictive:

Many students complete an MS degree, work under OPT, and then pursue an MBA to transition into management or entrepreneurship.

Others begin with one PhD field and discover a better fit in another, requiring a change of program.

Prohibiting such transitions contradicts the reality of U.S. higher education, where flexibility and interdisciplinary movement are strengths. It will also harm U.S. universities financially, as many MBA programs rely on international graduates with work experience.

Recommendation: XXXXX F-1 students to pursue additional degrees at the same or lower level if they demonstrate academic intent and sufficient funding, with appropriate SEVIS and DSO oversight.

3. OPT to PhD Transition and Risk of XXXXX

Currently, under D/S, students on OPT can smoothly transition to a PhD program by obtaining a new I-20 from a SEVP-certified institution. Under the proposed fixed-term system, students would also need to file an EOS with USCIS. Given that USCIS processing times can exceed several months, this creates a risk of status gaps or inadvertent unlawful presence if adjudications are delayed or denied.

Recommendation: Clarify that students transitioning from OPT to higher-level academic study will be considered to maintain status upon issuance of a new I-20 by a SEVP-certified institution, even if their EOS application is pending.

The NPRM proposes to shorten the grace period after completion of study or OPT from 60 days to 30 days. This time is critical for students to prepare for departure, secure admission into new programs, or file timely applications to change or extend status. Thirty days is insufficient to complete these processes, especially when administrative delays are common.

Recommendation: Retain the 60-day grace period for F-1 students to preserve continuity and fairness.

5. Administrative and Economic Costs

DHS’s own analysis estimates annualized costs of approximately $390 million over ten years for students, schools, and the government. These costs will reduce the attractiveness of U.S. higher education compared to other countries such as Canada, the UK, and Australia, which are actively competing for international talent with simpler visa regimes.

Recommendation: DHS should weigh the relatively small security benefits against the significant economic and reputational costs to U.S. higher education and make adjustments that preserve program integrity without undermining competitiveness.

Conclusion

The U.S. has long benefited from welcoming the world’s most talented students, many of whom contribute to American innovation, research, and economic growth. While oversight is important, the proposed rule as drafted will discourage international students from choosing the United States.

I urge DHS to revise the rule to:

Remove or expand the 4-year admission cap for long-duration programs.

XXXXX reasonable academic flexibility, including MBA and PhD transitions.

Ensure that OPT-to-study transitions do not create unlawful presence risks.

Retain the 60-day grace period.

Respectfully submitted，

E. Requirements for Admission, XXXXX, and Maintenance of Status of F Nonimmigrants

Sincerely,

comment_clean:
America's strength has always been tied to its ability to attract the world's brightest minds. International students are not just passive recipients of an American education; they are active contributors who invigorate our economy, strengthen our research institutions, and contribute directly to our technological and military prowess. The decisions we make today on immigration, especially policies for international students, will have profound and lasting consequences on the nation's future.

The Economic Engine of XXXXX
The financial contributions of international students are a critical pillar for many U.S. universities. By paying full tuition, they effectively subsidize the education of domestic students, helping to maintain academic programs and institutional stability. Their spending on housing, food, and other living expenses also injects billions of dollars into local economies annually. According to NAFSA, international students contributed over $43 billion to the U.S. economy in the 2XXXXX academic year and supported nearly 400,000 American jobs. This makes higher education a major U.S. export that generates a substantial trade surplus.

Indispensable Contributions to Scientific Research & Innovation
The role of foreign-born individuals in shaping America's technological landscape is a historical fact. From early 20th-century European immigrants to modern-day entrepreneurs like XXXXX (co-founder of Google) and XXXXX (founder of Tesla and SpaceX), immigrant founders have been central to creating many of the most influential companies of the last few decades. A study by the National Foundation for American XXXXX found that over half of U.S. billion-dollar startups had at least one immigrant founder. These companies generate wealth, drive innovation, and create jobs for Americans.

Beyond entrepreneurship, international students are indispensable to the American scientific and research ecosystem, making up a substantial portion of the graduate student population, particularly in critical STEM fields. Nearly half of all U.S. STEM doctoral and master's degrees are earned by international students, filling the high-skilled labor pipeline and pushing the boundaries of scientific discovery. Their contributions to fundamental research form the bedrock upon which future applications, including those in defense and aerospace, are built.

A Look Back: The Lessons of XXXXX
The policies of the late 1990s and early 2000s provide a stark case study in strategic versus reactive decision-making. The 1990s saw an increase in visas for high-skilled workers, which laid the groundwork for the burgeoning tech boom. However, the post-9/11 security measures, while necessary, led to complications for international students. This period highlights the dramatic consequences of subjective, fear-based decisions versus objective, strategic ones. A reactive approach, while seemingly prudent in the short term, can hobble a nation’s long-term competitive advantage.

Today, countries like China and those in Europe are actively vying for the same pool of intellectual talent by offering streamlined visa processes and clear paths to citizenship. The U.S. can no longer afford to be complacent. To ensure its continued strength and avoid a future that is less secure and prosperous, the U.S. must adopt policies that attract and retain the world's most capable minds.

One proposal for F-1 visa reform could limit visas to two years while offering a clear, expedited pathway to a green card for students with a GPA of 3.0 or higher. It would also serve as a quality control mechanism, ensuring that those who remain are truly committed to their education and to becoming productive members of society.

By providing a clear path to residency after a two-year period, this reform would incentivize students to focus on their studies from day one and become more deeply integrated into their communities. Establishing clear criteria—academic excellence, strong community ties, and adherence to regulations—would create a system that is both secure and beneficial for America's long-term success. The time has come to make strategic, rather than reactive, policy choices that will secure America's intellectual and economic leadership for generations to come.

title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comment_clean:
XXXXX Summary

I respectfully oppose the Department of Homeland Security’s proposal to replace “duration of status” (D/S) with fixed admission periods for F, J, and I nonimmigrants. As an international student and software engineer, I would be directly and negatively affected. The proposed rule creates unnecessary administrative burdens, risks repeated interruptions to my education, and undermines the very principles of opportunity, innovation, and exchange that the United States has long championed. DHS should retain the D/S framework, which has worked effectively for decades, while strengthening existing oversight tools like SEVIS.

1. XXXXX and Mental Health Concerns
The proposed rule would force students like me to apply repeatedly for extensions of stay (EOS), creating major uncertainty and interruptions in our education. DHS itself acknowledges that F-1 students may face program delays due to academic probation, suspension, or other reasons, and considers these “generally unacceptable” for extensions (Proposed XXXXX, p. 123, 8 CFR 214.2(f)). This is particularly harmful for students with disabilities such as ADHD, who may need additional time or flexibility. Instead of being supported, we would be penalized by shortened timelines and bureaucratic hurdles.

2. Financial and Opportunity Costs
DHS estimates the rule would impose annualized costs of $390 million to $392 million globally, with at least $86 million to $88 million directly on U.S. institutions and students (Proposed XXXXX, p. 104). For individual students, this means repeated filing fees, legal expenses, and loss of valuable study time. Each extension carries not only direct monetary cost but also the stress of possible denials, delays, and school interruptions. As someone who works while studying, I depend on the continuity of my education to apply knowledge from school into my professional life, and vice versa. Breaking this cycle undermines both learning and productivity.

3. XXXXX on Innovation and the “American Dream”
The United States has long attracted global talent by offering a flexible system that allows students to pursue their fields of passion, change majors if necessary, and combine study with practical experience. The proposed rule would restrict graduate students from changing programs once enrolled (Proposed XXXXX, p. 121, 8 CFR 214.2(f)(6)(iii)), eliminating the ability to adjust academic paths—a critical part of the educational process. This rigidity is inconsistent with the American tradition of self-improvement and innovation. For me, the chance to study different programs and integrate them into my work is central to why I chose the U.S. If this flexibility is removed, the system fails to live up to its promise.

4. Practical Alternatives
Rather than imposing blanket fixed terms, DHS should:

Retain D/S while strengthening SEVIS reporting and compliance reviews.

Provide a safe harbor so that students who timely file extension applications do not face unlawful presence or study interruptions.

Expand disability accommodations, allowing program extensions for medical or learning-related needs without penalty.

Target enforcement against fraud with data-driven methods rather than penalizing the vast majority of compliant students.

Conclusion
The proposed rule would not meaningfully increase national security or compliance but would impose severe educational, financial, and psychological costs on law-abiding students. It would reduce the United States’ attractiveness as a global leader in higher education and innovation. I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and retain the duration of status framework, with targeted improvements in oversight.

Respectfully submitted,
Software Engineer and International Student

title: Comment Submitted by Nick Xu
comment_clean:
I write to highlight several ways the proposed rule could harm U.S. citizens—students, workers, consumers, taxpayers, and communities—by shifting F, J, and I nonimmigrants from “duration of status” (D/S) to fixed admission periods (generally capped at four years) with new extension-of-stay (EOS) requirements and earlier unlawful-presence triggers tied to I-94 expiration.

1) Higher costs for U.S. schools and small sponsors that spill over to American students and families

DHS’s own analysis anticipates substantial compliance and administrative burdens on U.S. institutions and sponsors, including thousands of small entities. Those costs (e.g., staff time, training, systems, EOS processing support) will be passed along through higher tuition, fees, or reduced services that U.S. students and their families ultimately pay.

2) Reduced research capacity and fewer course sections that Americans rely on

International F-1 graduate students and J-1 scholars teach and conduct research across U.S. universities. The proposal’s fixed end dates and more frequent EOS risk interruptions, status lapses, and travel/visa churn. When TAs/RAs can’t start or must pause mid-semester, universities often cut sections or delay labs, degrading instructional quality for U.S. undergraduates and slowing research that benefits American industry and taxpayers. The rule itself acknowledges large affected populations (approx. 2.1 million F, J, I participants annually), so even modest friction can have outsized effects on American students.

3) Physician shortages and health access for Americans—especially in rural and underserved areas

J-1 exchange visitors include physicians in U.S. training programs. XXXXX uncertainty, earlier unlawful-presence accrual upon I-94 expiry, and EOS complexity can deter or disrupt placements. Americans—particularly in shortage areas—may face longer wait times and diminished access if programs struggle to recruit/retain trainees and fellows. (This flows logically from the rule’s universal application to J-1 categories and its emphasis on stricter timelines and unlawful-presence triggers.)

4) Local economic harm to U.S. communities and small businesses

International students and exchange visitors support local housing markets and small businesses (food, transport, retail). DHS flags potential declines in international enrollment; that reduces spending in college towns and cities nationwide. Fewer customers mean lost revenue and jobs for U.S. workers. Small entities already bear compliance costs under the proposal; revenue losses compound the impact.

5) More USCIS and CBP workload → longer queues for everyone, including U.S. citizens

By replacing D/S with fixed dates and requiring more EOS filings, the proposal increases adjudications and port-of-entry interactions. DHS acknowledges it considered (and rejected) shorter max stays because of workload concerns—admitting that the policy design trades compliance checks for processing volume. XXXXX volume can slow processing for U.S. citizens (e.g., Americans who need other USCIS services) due to finite agency capacity.

6) Risks to press access and timely news for Americans

The rule applies to I-visa foreign media. XXXXX admission periods and earlier unlawful-presence accrual risks can create coverage gaps when journalists must depart, wait for EOS, or navigate new timing pitfalls. Americans consequently receive less timely reporting on international events, with fewer foreign correspondents operating in the U.S. public sphere.

7) Greater legal exposure and humanitarian fallout that communities must absorb

Under D/S, minor school or program hiccups didn’t automatically trigger unlawful presence. Tying status to a fixed date means unlawful presence begins at I-94 expiry, increasing bars to reentry and producing abrupt status crises (e.g., a delayed thesis defense or administrative error). Local governments, nonprofits, and U.S. neighbors often shoulder the human and administrative fallout (legal aid, emergency housing, school disruptions for U.S. citizen children in mixed-status families).

8) Competitiveness losses that ultimately reduce benefits to U.S. citizens

The United States competes globally for talent. A rigid four-year cap, additional EOS friction, and earlier unlawful-presence penalties deter top students, researchers, doctors, teachers, and journalists from choosing the U.S. Lower enrollment and participation degrade academic programs, diminish innovation, and reduce long-term tax revenue and job creation that benefit U.S. citizens. DHS itself notes potential reductions in fee revenue and enrollments.

Overburden an already stretched USCIS

Increased Administrative and Financial Burdens on Students: The proposal requires F-1 students to file EOS applications with USCIS for stays beyond the initial fixed period (up to 4 years, tied to program length). As a student already managing tuition, living expenses, and academic demands, this adds significant costs (e.g., filing fees, biometrics, and potential legal assistance) and time-consuming paperwork. Processing delays could leave students in limbo, unable to plan ahead, and force them to pay for extensions even for minor program adjustments like thesis delays. Disruption to XXXXX and Progress: Under the new rules, F-1 students would face restrictions on changing educational objectives, transferring schools without completing the first academic year, or pursuing programs at the same or lower educational levels. For instance, prohibiting program changes at the graduate level or requiring completion of one program before starting another at a higher level limits intellectual exploration. As someone pursuing advanced studies, I value the ability to adapt my research or switch fields based on evolving interests or opportunities (e.g., from a master's to a PhD). These rigid rules could force students to abandon promising paths or rush through programs, harming educational quality and innovation, which contradicts the U.S.'s reputation as a hub for flexible, world-class education.
Heightened Uncertainty and Mental Health Stress: The shift from D/S to fixed dates introduces constant uncertainty about visa status, as EOS approvals are discretionary and could be denied due to minor issues like academic probation (which the proposal deems generally unacceptable for extensions). Currently, D/S allows compliance through school reporting without fixed end dates, reducing such risks. Students might face status violations if an EOS is delayed beyond the admission period, even if filed timely—potentially resulting in deportation, bans, or career-ending consequences. This punitive approach treats all students as potential risks, ignoring that the vast majority (over 1.6 million F-1 admissions in 2023) comply fully, and overlooks SEVIS's real-time tracking capabilities.
Unnecessary and XXXXX Solution to Perceived Problems: DHS cites national security and fraud concerns, but the existing D/S system, bolstered by SEVIS since post-9/11 reforms, already provides robust oversight through mandatory reporting by designated school officials (DSOs) on enrollment, address changes, and program completion. Targeted enforcement (e.g., audits of high-risk cases) would be more effective than overhauling a system that has worked for decades, especially since the proposal's own economic analysis estimates annualized costs of $390-392 million, much of which falls on students and schools.
Negative Impact on U.S. Universities, XXXXX, and XXXXX: International students contribute billions to the U.S. economy through tuition, housing, and innovation (e.g., in STEM fields). This rule could deter prospective students by making the U.S. less attractive compared to countries like Canada or Australia, which offer more flexible visa systems. For U.S. institutions, it means added administrative work for DSOs (e.g., updating Forms I-20 for extensions) and potential enrollment drops, harming diversity and revenue. As a contributor to campus life and future U.S. workforce (via OPT), I believe this erodes America's edge in attracting global talent, contradicting goals of fostering international exchange.

Operationally, the policy multiplies burdens precisely as other new processes (fixed admission periods and extension-of-stay filings) are added. Students seeking legitimate, skills-focused programs would face automatic denials or ambiguous level determinations. DSOs would draft level-justification memos; USCIS would see more edge-case filings and appeals; schools would divert staff away from advising and research toward compliance. This increases friction and the risk of status gaps without improving integrity.

The broader public impacts are real. Interdisciplinary fluency is central to U.S. innovation—software with design for accessibility, statistics with public policy for evidence-based governance, ethics with AI for trustworthy systems, architecture with sustainability for climate-aligned construction. Preventing lateral upskilling slows translation from ideas to deployment, weakens team literacy inside organizations, and narrows the talent pipeline that employers—from startups to hospitals to public agencies—depend on. The likeliest outcome is talent choosing jurisdictions that welcome modular learning, weakening U.S. competitiveness.

Equity concerns loom large. By privileging only “higher” degrees, the rule penalizes students who would benefit from shorter, lower-cost programs to gain specific competencies or pivot responsibly between fields. Those with fewer resources will feel compelled to pursue more expensive degrees they do not need, simply to comply. That dynamic inflates debt, misallocates educational resources, and reduces socioeconomic diversity.

There are reliance and transition issues as well. Many students and universities planned around modular add-ons: learning analytics after education, UX after computer science, public finance after economics, sustainability management after architecture. Transition from XXXXX’s → OPT/STEM OPT → Ph.D. (expired visa, lawful under D/S)

Background under current rules.
One of the most common academic pathways for international students is to pursue a U.S. XXXXX’s degree, then use Optional Practical Training (OPT) and the 24-month STEM OPT extension to gain professional experience and afterward enroll in a U.S. Ph.D. program. This progression is natural and encouraged by universities because students arrive at their doctoral studies with stronger professional grounding. Under the current D/S system, such students remain in valid status throughout the process even if their visa stamp has expired, as long as their SEVIS record is active and the Designated School Official (DSO) confirms full-time enrollment. The D/S framework therefore allows continuity without repeated government filings, relying instead on DSOs as trained compliance monitors.

How the proposal changes things.
The NPRM would set fixed admission periods (commonly 4 years for F-1 students). For a XXXXX’s graduate entering a Ph.D. that may last 6–7 years, this means their status would expire mid-program. The student would then have to file for an Extension of Stay (“EOS”) with USCIS. Because visa stamps can only be renewed abroad, most of these students will already have expired visa foils but still be lawful under D/S. Fixed terms now put them at risk: if the “EOS” is delayed or denied, the student could fall out of status despite being fully enrolled. The proposal thereby shifts lawful presence from a predictable SEVIS-based model to one dependent on unpredictable USCIS adjudications.

Why this matters for students.
•Academic continuity: Ph.D. students often work on long-term research projects (e.g., 5-year NSF-funded experiments, longitudinal clinical trials). An “EOS” denial mid-program could destroy years of work.
•Employment/assistantships: Graduate assistants, research assistants, and teaching assistants’ roles that sustain many departments depend on continuous enrollment. Losing status interrupts payroll, health insurance, and tuition remission.
•Equity concerns: Wealthier students can afford attorneys and premium processing; students from less-resourced backgrounds cannot, creating inequities unrelated to merit.
•Mental health & stability: Constant fear of losing status undermines well-being and academic performance.

Why this matters for universities.
•Research disruption: International Ph.D. students represent the majority in some STEM fields. For example, NSF data show that over 50% of U.S. engineering Ph.D.’s are international. Interruptions harm labs, delay grant deliverables, and erode institutional competitiveness.
•Financial loss: Universities depend on tuition revenue, RA/TA contributions, and grant output. Losing a single student mid-program cascades into lost income and delayed publications.
•Administrative burden: DSOs and graduate program staff would spend significant time assisting students with USCIS filings rather than academic advising.

Why this matters for the U.S. economy.
•Workforce pipeline: Many students who follow the XXXXX’s → OPT → Ph.D. pathway become permanent residents through EB-2 or EB-1 categories and contribute to high-skill labor markets. Disrupting this flow shrinks the U.S. innovation pipeline.
•Competitiveness: Canada, the UK, and Germany are actively expanding post-study work rights. Adding new risks makes the U.S. less attractive.

Case example.
Consider a student who earns an M.S. in Mechanical Engineering, spends 3 years on OPT/STEM OPT working at a turbine manufacturer, then enrolls in a Ph.D. in Energy Systems. Under D/S, their status is lawful until their Ph.D. completion. Under the proposal, their 4-year admission would expire during year 5 of the Ph.D., forcing an “EOS”. If USCIS delays processing, their RA position funding a DOE project could be voided, the lab loses continuity, and the student may face unlawful presence despite full compliance.

Current benefit to preserve.
The D/S framework aligns lawful presence with actual academic progress, as monitored by DSOs, and shields compliant students from bureaucratic timing failures.

Recommendations.
1.Grandfathering: Students who already lawfully advanced from XXXXX’s → OPT/STEM OPT → Ph.D. under D/S should retain continuity through program completion.
2.DSO deference: USCIS should treat DSO certification of enrollment as primary evidence of progression, avoiding redundant scrutiny.
3.Automatic continuation: Status and work authorization should continue automatically if an “EOS” is filed on time, mirroring cap-gap logic, so students don’t face stop-work orders during adjudication.
4.Transparent timelines: USCIS should publish and meet service standards (e.g., 120 days adjudication) to protect students from harmful delays.

The Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) authorizes students to remain for the duration of a full course of study (§101(a)(15)(F)) and does not mandate rigid year limits. The D/S system, in place since 1978, was specifically designed to reduce administrative burden and align with this statutory design. The proposed fixed term is inconsistent with congressional intent and risks being arbitrary under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).

Harm to Educational Programs:
Most U.S. doctoral programs require 5–7 years, and many professional programs (medicine, dentistry, pharmacy) take 6–8 years. A four-year ceiling would force nearly all such students to apply for extensions, creating unnecessary bureaucracy, increasing USCIS backlogs, and introducing legal uncertainty.

Damage to OPT and H-1B Pathways:
OPT, including STEM OPT, is codified in existing regulations and provides a vital bridge to H-1B employment. Shorter admission periods would disrupt the “cap-gap” protection recognized under INA §214(g)(3), leaving students at risk of unlawful presence despite following lawful processes.

Infringement on Academic Freedom:
The rule’s prohibition on lateral degree changes or second-degree enrollment intrudes into academic decision-making, which is reserved for accredited institutions and the Department of Education. Graduate students frequently shift disciplines in response to research needs and career goals; restricting this undermines the flexibility and innovation that are hallmarks of U.S. higher education.

Unnecessary Burdens and XXXXX:
DHS justifies the rule by citing isolated fraud or security cases. Yet these risks are already addressed by SEVIS oversight, school accreditation, and targeted enforcement actions. A blanket shift from D/S to fixed terms would penalize millions of law-abiding students and scholars while offering little measurable security improvement.

Recommendations

Withdraw the proposed fixed-term framework and retain the Duration of Status (D/S) system.

Preserve existing OPT and STEM OPT structures, including cap-gap protection for H-1B applicants.

Allow legitimate academic flexibility, including second degrees and program changes, consistent with the INA.

Focus enforcement on fraud detection and SEVIS monitoring rather than imposing broad restrictions on compliant students.

Conclusion
The proposed rule is inconsistent with statute, harmful to U.S. higher education, and unnecessarily burdensome to both DHS and the public. It would deter talented students and researchers, weaken the global competitiveness of American universities, and create administrative backlogs without tangible security gains. For these reasons, I strongly urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule in its entirety.

In conclusion, the NPRM’s fixed-date architecture, academic-mobility bans, and shortened grace period would increase adjudication load and status failures without commensurate benefits—while undermining a proven engine of U.S. education and economic growth. A few features of the proposed limits on visas to study at the same or lower level have a significant potential to cause unintended effects on bona fide students, particularly ones at reputable institutions, that ought to warrant changes to the proposed rule before it is finalized.

First, the proposed rule's provisions regarding limits on pursuing study at the same or lower level does not adequately address complications that may arise from individuals with PhDs who subsequently undertake a professional degree. For example, a scientist might obtain a biochemistry PhD and then subsequently undertake an MD to pursue a career in medicine. Conversely, a doctor with an MD degree might subsequently decide to pursue a PhD in order to prepare for a career in research or teaching. The rules should clarify that a professional doctorate is regarded as being in a different category to a PhD and that pursuing one does not preclude pursuing another.

Second, certain masters-level degrees in professional fields require a professional doctorate as a prerequisite. For example, a student applying to NYU's well-known LLM degree in tax would very likely have a JD degree (or foreign equivalent). Despite being called a masters, this is a higher level of study than the professional doctorate. The rules should either clarify the professional doctorate is a lower-level degree to the post-professional-doctorate masters degree or provide ample waiver authority to address this situation.

Third, rules regarding the same or higher level of study should be attentive to differences between different countries' terminology for levels of study. In certain countries, such as France or the Universities of XXXXX and Cambridge in England, a degree with the title of masters may equivalent to a U.S. bachelor's degree. Similarly, for historical reasons, XXXXX's masters-level degrees in law or theology are called bachelor's.

Fourth, the proposed restriction on graduate students changing their program of study is likely to create two noteworthy problems. First, the rules should permit a "change" that is effectively a continuation of the same program. For example, if a student applies for a PhD proposing to write a dissertation on a particular topic but, due to a change in the supervising professor, the same proposal gets reclassified by the university as, say, XXXXX rather than Engineering, that should not be considered a change of program of study. Second, dual degree programs - such as, say, being admitted to an MD program and then applying to do a joint MD-PhD, or applying to a JD program and then applying to make it a JD-MBA instead - should not be considered a change of program of study; the student is still undertaking their original program, but doing a dual program as well.

Fifth, the rules should provide relatively robust authority to waive course-change and same-or-higher-level rules where it is in the national interest to do so, so that immigration officers have discretion to address idiosyncratic situations - for example, a PhD graduate who needs to take a post-baccalaureate pre-med program in order to gain admission to an MD program. This type of waiver authority will help ensure that the best and the brightest who are attending bona fide, well-reputed universities can be distinguished from people who are effectively abusing the F-1 program through dubious programs that are not really courses of study.

Finally, as an additional security measure, DHS should consider developing a biometric identity card for students (similar to an EAD card). Other countries, such as the UK, have biometric identity cards for people on student visas. Moreover, developing a card as proof of alien registration for student visa holders could reduce the need for visa holders to constantly carry their passport and I-20, which has a tendency to lead to lost passports and additional paperwork burden on the student, DHS, and State to process replacement visas for a new passport.

I am writing to provide comments regarding the proposed rule entitled “Establishing a Fixed Time Period of Admission and an Extension of XXXXX for Nonimmigrant Academic Students, XXXXX, and Representatives of Foreign Information Media” published on August 28, 2025.

While I understand the Department of Homeland Security’s intent to strengthen the integrity of the student visa system, I respectfully urge the Department to reconsider or clarify the provision that would restrict F-1 nonimmigrants from pursuing another program at the same or a lower educational level after completing one in the United States.

1. The MBA is distinct from other master’s programs and often pursued after work experience.
An MBA program is not merely “another master’s degree” at the same level. It is a professional, leadership-focused degree that requires years of prior work experience and serves a very different educational and career purpose compared to an academic master’s program such as a Master of Science in Finance, XXXXX, or Engineering. It is very common—and indeed encouraged—worldwide for individuals to pursue a specialized academic master’s degree early in their careers, work in their field, and later return for an MBA to transition into senior management or entrepreneurship. Preventing such students from pursuing an MBA in the U.S. would place American business schools at a global disadvantage.

2. Restricting second master’s programs undermines U.S. competitiveness.
The United States has long been the top destination for international students, who bring talent, cultural diversity, and economic benefits. Many top MBA programs—such as those at Harvard, XXXXX, XXXXX, and others—attract mid-career professionals who already hold a graduate degree. If DHS were to prohibit F-1 visas for such students, they would be forced to pursue MBA programs in Europe, Canada, or Asia instead, resulting in a significant loss of tuition revenue, entrepreneurial potential, and long-term connections that benefit the U.S. economy.

3. A more balanced approach is possible.
Instead of a blanket prohibition, DHS could consider:

Allowing F-1 eligibility for second master’s degrees when there is a substantial gap of work experience between programs (e.g., 3–5 years).

Recognizing MBAs as a distinct category of professional degree, given their unique curriculum and career outcomes.

Requiring additional documentation (career goals, work history, program differentiation) rather than denying eligibility altogether.

Conclusion
In sum, many international professionals—myself included—follow a very typical path: complete a specialized master’s degree, work for several years in industry, and then return for an MBA. This is a rational, career-driven decision, not a misuse of the F-1 system. The proposed restriction, if implemented without clarification or exception, would unintentionally harm U.S. higher education and the economy by driving away precisely the kind of globally-minded, experienced professionals that American MBA programs are designed to serve.

Thank you for considering this comment. I respectfully urge DHS to revise or clarify the proposed rule to ensure that international students with legitimate academic and professional goals, especially those pursuing MBAs, can continue to contribute to U.S. universities and society.

Executive Summary
As a university faculty member, I strongly oppose the proposed rule replacing “duration of status” (D/S) with fixed admission periods for students and exchange visitors. This change would create instability for international students, disrupt teaching and research programs, and impose administrative burdens on both students and universities. The Department’s own analysis acknowledges millions of additional filings and significant costs (Proposed XXXXX PDF, p. 209), yet fails to consider the academic consequences of introducing rigid visa deadlines into long and often unpredictable educational pathways.

1. Academic Disruption of Long-Term Programs
Graduate and doctoral programs often extend beyond two or four years, with research timelines that cannot be neatly predicted. Students conducting fieldwork, dissertation research, or lab-based projects frequently require program extensions. Under fixed admission terms, students will face mid-program visa expirations, requiring extensions that risk interruptions to their studies. The Proposed XXXXX does not address how such interruptions would affect timely degree completion (Proposed XXXXX PDF, pp. 40–41).

2. XXXXX on Universities and Advising Offices
The Department estimates 2.5 million new annual filings and nearly $100 million in added costs (Proposed XXXXX PDF, p. 209). Much of this burden will fall not only on students but also on universities, which must dedicate staff to process and support extension filings. University international offices, already resource-limited, will be forced to divert staff away from academic advising and research support to handle immigration paperwork. These indirect costs are not captured in the Department’s analysis.

3. Undermining U.S. Educational Competitiveness
The United States has long been the leading destination for international students, in part because of the flexibility and stability provided by D/S. Peer countries such as Canada, the U.K., and Australia provide clear multi-year study authorizations aligned with program length. By imposing unpredictable mid-program visa deadlines, the U.S. risks losing top talent to competitor nations. The Department does not present data to counter this risk, leaving a significant gap in its assessment.

Practical Alternatives
Instead of replacing D/S entirely, DHS could:

Retain duration of status (D/S) for academic programs, while increasing targeted compliance reviews.

Implement a safe harbor for students with timely-filed extensions to avoid disruption of studies.

Improve data collection on academic program length and completion timelines before altering policy.

Conclusion
From the perspective of a faculty member responsible for teaching and mentoring international students, this rule would create academic instability, administrative overload, and reduced global competitiveness. A balanced policy should preserve D/S while strengthening oversight mechanisms that address specific risks without harming legitimate students and universities.

Administrative burden: 2.5M filings, $99.3M/10 years (Proposed XXXXX PDF, p. 209).

CPT/academic program disruptions noted (Proposed XXXXX PDF, pp. 40–41).

Missing analysis on university advising burden and international competitiveness.

comment_clean:
Introduction: As a higher education professional with 17 years of experience supporting international students through academic program completion, I write to oppose this proposed rule. My work with Designated School Officials and direct observation of student academic progression provides firsthand insight into how this regulation would fundamentally disrupt effective educational oversight while imposing massive taxpayer costs for no security benefit.
Background: This comment addresses the proposed changes requiring F, J, and I visa holders to transition from "duration of status" (D/S) admissions to fixed four-year periods with mandatory Extension of Status (EOS) applications through USCIS, prohibiting program changes in the first year, eliminating same-level degree options, and shifting oversight from knowledgeable local school officials to federal adjudicators lacking higher education training.
Analysis: The agency has catastrophically underestimated this proposal's fiscal impact on American taxpayers. Currently, SEVP operates as a self-funded system through I-901 fees paid by students, costing taxpayers minimal amounts. This proposal would require taxpayer funding for hundreds of thousands of new EOS adjudications annually, necessitating massive USCIS adjudicator hiring, extensive CBP retraining, mandatory HR staff retraining nationwide, and system updates DHS has promised since 2010 but consistently failed to deliver.
The security rationale contradicts operational reality and relies too heavily on technology solutions. XXXXX and SEVP representatives already conduct comprehensive monitoring through daily student interactions that identify concerning behaviors no paperwork review could capture. Federal adjudicators reviewing transcripts and applications cannot detect espionage, fraud, or security threats - behavioral assessments require personal interaction and institutional knowledge, not distant bureaucratic paperwork reviews. The proposal's reliance on SEVIS system updates and complex technological tracking ignores DHS's consistent failure to deliver promised system improvements over the past 14 years.
Educational impacts are severe and ignore fundamental learning principles. XXXXX's degree completion statistics demonstrate six-year average timelines due to legitimate academic factors: varying credit requirements across majors, academic exploration, and normal progression challenges. The minimum 12-credit-hour does not legally require students to achieve 120 credits in four years, as expected by this rule. Education involves learning from mistakes and failures - students should be allowed to fail courses and recover without deportation threats. Prohibiting first-year transfers forces students into potentially unsuitable programs after experiencing just one semester, while preventing same-level additional degrees contradicts professional development in complex industries requiring multiple XXXXX's Degrees.
Current USCIS processing times of 60-210 days will become catastrophic with massive application volume increases. The 240-day processing exception window spans two complete academic semesters, anticipating such a delay ignores the prolonged legal limbo students encounter while remaining legally in the US with valid pending applications. CBP officers will face administrative chaos calculating fixed end dates, maximum time limits, varying grace periods, and pending applications - complexity far beyond simple D/S determinations that will generate costly entry errors and wrongful exclusions.
Historical precedent confirms this approach's failure. A previous administration attempted identical reforms but abandoned them in the same term as they were ineffective and unworkable, returning to the D/S system that has successfully operated for 34 years.
Recommendations: Withdraw this proposal entirely. Instead, enhance the existing SEVP framework by providing additional resources and training to local officials already performing effective oversight without relying on complex technological solutions. XXXXX chronic SEVP regional representative vacancies. XXXXX direct human oversight capabilities through increased DSO training and consistent regional SEVP staffing rather than replacing knowledgeable local oversight with distant federal bureaucracy. XXXXX D/S admissions that accommodate educational realities including normal academic progression and program exploration.
Conclusion: This proposal transforms an efficient, self-funded system into a taxpayer-funded bureaucracy achieving no security benefits while harming educational institutions, legitimate students, and American communities. The recommendation remains clear: withdraw this costly proposal that ignores educational realities and strengthen existing effective oversight mechanisms without burdening American taxpayers or forcing students into rigid academic pathways that contradict sound educational principles.

Specifically, the rule would ban international graduate students from transferring or changing programs once enrolled. This restriction undermines labor protections, creates inequities within graduate employment, and reduces the competitiveness of U.S. higher education.

1. Negative Impacts on Graduate Employees

Graduate education often involves evolving research interests and, in some cases, the need to change programs or institutions. The proposed ban on program changes for graduate-level F-1 students would deny international graduate employees this flexibility (Proposed XXXXX, p. 117–118, §214.2(f)). For those working as teaching assistants (TAs) or research assistants (RAs), the inability to transfer worsens workplace vulnerability. If an advisor imposes unreasonable workloads or unfair conditions, international students would have no option but to accept them. This loss of exit options weakens protections for all graduate employees, including U.S. citizens, because it diminishes the collective ability to resist exploitative arrangements.

This inequity undermines the principle that all graduate employees—regardless of citizenship status—deserve equal treatment and workplace protections.

Practical Alternatives

Instead of banning transfers for international graduate students, DHS should:

a) Allow transfers and program changes, subject to proper SEVIS reporting and oversight, rather than outright prohibitions.

b) Create safe harbor provisions ensuring students who initiate a transfer in good faith are not penalized with unlawful presence.

c) Enhance compliance monitoring of schools and Designated School Officials (DSOs) to prevent abuse without punishing students who need academic mobility.

Conclusion

Protecting the rights of U.S. graduate employees requires equal protections for all graduate employees. Prohibiting international graduate students from transferring programs will entrench inequities, weaken workplace protections, and harm U.S. competitiveness. The rule would impose large, unnecessary administrative burdens and backlogs, create avoidable status-loss risks, and undermine U.S. higher education, research, and workforce competitiveness.

First, the rule creates large, unfunded administrative costs and backlog risks. Shifting millions of routine academic extensions from Designated School Officials (DSOs) and Responsible Officers (ROs) to USCIS will significantly increase filings and wait times. USCIS’s own data and public reports show persistent, system-wide backlogs and fluctuating completion capacity; piling mandatory extensions onto this pipeline is likely to slow adjudications further. Besides, when extensions are routed through USCIS, any surge, staffing shortfall, or biometrics scheduling delay can force students and scholars into gaps in status or work authorization, disrupting research labs, teaching duties, and time-sensitive training.

Second, the rule will deter talent and reduce economic and academic benefits. International students reached ~1.13 million in AY 2023/24, including record graduate and OPT participation, supporting U.S. campuses and local economies. NAFSA estimates that international students sustain hundreds of thousands of U.S. jobs and contribute tens of billions of dollars annually. XXXXX uncertainty and new extension hurdles will depress these gains. For scientific research, foreign-born talent constitutes a substantial share of the U.S. STEM workforce and advanced degree graduates; many remain and contribute to innovation ecosystems. Policies that heighten uncertainty at routine academic milestones will divert this talent to competitor countries.

Third, the rule increases status-loss risk without demonstrated security gains. D/S worked for decades by tying lawful presence to ongoing compliance verified in SEVIS by DSOs/ROs. Under the proposed shift, a missed filing, delayed biometrics, or a slow adjudication at the end of a term could trigger immediate unlawful presence accrual after the I-94 end date plus the shortened 30-day grace period—an outcome often unrelated to any genuine compliance or security problem. The NPRM does not provide compelling evidence that mass-routing routine extensions to USCIS will yield proportionate integrity benefits relative to the new risks it creates.

Fourth, the rule causes practical harms to academic progress and training. PhD Timelines Often Exceed Four Years. The proposed four-year cap will force mid-program USCIS filings for many graduate students, introducing delay and cost at sensitive research stages. The NPRM’s conditions on filing during the 30-day grace period restrict practical training and employment while extensions are pending—disrupting lab work, employer onboarding, and project deliverables.

In conclusion, because the proposed rule imposes large administrative and economic costs, heightens status-loss risks, and undermines U.S. academic and innovation leadership—without demonstrating commensurate integrity benefits—I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposal. At minimum, DHS should retain D/S and adopt targeted, risk-based oversight; or, if fixed admissions are maintained, extend admission lengths to match typical degree durations, restore a 60-day grace period, preserve seamless practical training, and keep routine in-program extensions with DSOs/ROs rather than USCIS.

XXXXX Department of Homeland Security,

Thank you for allowing the public to respond to this proposal. I understand and respect DHS’s effort to maintain the integrity of the F-1 visa program and to prevent individuals from misusing student status. However, I am concerned about the proposed rule that would block students from pursuing a second master’s degree or another degree at the same level.

As it stands, the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) authorizes international students to pursue a “full course of study” at accredited institutions so long as they maintain proper status. The law does not restrict students from seeking more than one degree at the same level. In addition, the Higher Education Act reflects a broader national commitment to expanding access to higher education in the United States. A blanket ban on second master’s degrees seems to go further than what the law provides, and in doing so, risks closing off legitimate academic paths.

There are many valid reasons a student might want to pursue another master’s in a different discipline. For example, someone with a background in mathematics might later wish to gain advanced training in computer science to stay competitive in today’s economy. Under the current proposal, that pathway would be blocked—even though it is educationally meaningful and economically relevant. Instead of preventing abuse, such a restriction could end up discouraging talented students from staying in the U.S. higher education system.

For this reason, I urge DHS to reconsider the scope of this provision. A more balanced approach would be to limit only duplicate degrees in the same or substantially similar field at the same level, while allowing students to pursue a degree in a different academic discipline. This would prevent misuse of status without penalizing those who are genuinely trying to expand their education and adapt to changing professional demands.

In my view, such an adjustment would better align with both the letter of the INA and the long-standing U.S. tradition of promoting access to education. It would also help the country continue to attract capable, ambitious students who ultimately contribute to American innovation and competitiveness.

Thank you for considering these comments. I hope DHS will take this perspective into account as it revises the proposal.

The proposed change conflicts with longstanding practice under the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA). University international student offices (ISSS/OIS) already face heavy compliance burdens under SEVIS. Moving to fixed timelines will dramatically increase their workload, requiring constant updates, I-20 reissuance, and filings with USCIS. For employers, uncertainty about whether a student can lawfully complete a program or continue OPT/STEM OPT authorization creates additional compliance risks, reducing hiring of international talent.

The proposal applies a “one-size-fits-all” rule to a highly diverse set of programs and student circumstances. It does not account for:
•PhD and research programs that routinely exceed 4–6 years;
•Professional programs with required internships or licensing timelines;
•Students with health issues or gap semesters;
•Transfer students or those changing majors;
•OPT/STEM OPT participants, whose lawful stay is tied to completing degree requirements.

Adding instability through fixed timelines will discourage prospective students from choosing U.S. institutions, driving them to competitor countries like Canada, the U.K., or Australia, which offer clearer and more stable visa frameworks. On an individual level, students would face higher costs from repeated filings and unrecoverable tuition if forced to leave mid-degree. Employers would lose access to skilled workers during OPT and STEM OPT periods, undermining the U.S. labor market in technology, finance, and consulting.

Conclusion & XXXXX

•Provide clear exemptions for long-term programs such as PhDs;
•Ensure protections for students on OPT/STEM OPT;
•Conduct a full economic and administrative impact assessment before finalization.

I respectfully oppose the NPRM because it (1) lacks a persuasive evidence base for sweeping structural changes, (2) does not demonstrate a least-burdensome approach consistent with modern regulatory review principles, (3) underestimates paperwork and processing burdens that will overwhelm USCIS queues and academic calendars, and (4) increases legal and compliance risk without clear oversight gains.

1) Thin evidence for categorical changes
The proposal replaces D/S with fixed end dates, pushes routine, DSO-validated continuations into USCIS Extension of Stay adjudications, and adds categorical prohibitions (such as limits on program changes and same-level study for F-1). The rule does not show that existing SEVIS controls are inadequate or that targeted fixes would fail. Major reversals of long-standing practice warrant stronger, quantitative justification.

2) Least-burdensome rulemaking not demonstrated
Regulatory review principles require agencies to consider benefits, costs, distributional effects, and reasonable alternatives. Here, narrower options—annual SEVIS validations, risk-based audits, and clear triggers for USCIS review—are available but not meaningfully evaluated. Selecting a universal USCIS routing plus categorical bans, without a side-by-side analysis of lighter-touch approaches, is not a least-burdensome path.

3) Small-entity impacts are underexplored
Graduate enrollment is tightly coupled to local economies and many smaller institutions. An adequate small-entity analysis should examine alternatives that keep D/S with enhanced validations or limit USCIS filings to exception-based cases, thereby reducing downstream effects on schools and host communities.

4) Predictable processing bottlenecks
I-539 timelines already fluctuate and can span months. Moving time-sensitive student continuations into those queues—potentially with biometrics—will create registration, assistantship, CPT/OPT, and travel gaps that campuses cannot reliably plan around. “Automatic continuation” helps only partially; many decisions hinge on timely adjudication that service centers cannot guarantee.

5) Transition and legal risk
Intricate transition rules, first-year limits, grace-period nuances, and travel-while-pending scenarios raise the odds of inconsistent application and accidental noncompliance. DSOs and students will be forced to synchronize I-20/DS-2019 dates, fixed I-94 terms, filing windows, and campus systems. Increased inadvertent lapses undermine the oversight objective.

6) Reliance interests and program stability
Institutions have structured admissions cycles, course sequencing, staffing, and funding around settled D/S practice. Reviving a fixed-term concept without squarely addressing reliance interests and earlier criticisms risks instability for campuses and students alike. At minimum, the agency should explain what has changed in evidence and operations to justify a different outcome.

A better path—feasible alternatives to analyze

Keep D/S with targeted checks. XXXXX annual SEVIS validations and risk-based school audits; use data-driven triggers (e.g., anomalous transfer or extension patterns) for USCIS review instead of routing all continuations.

Limit categorical bans. Allow same-level study when the new program is materially different and DSO-justified; curb serial enrollment with objective criteria rather than bright-line prohibitions.

Reserve USCIS EOS for exceptions. Keep DSO-managed extensions under strengthened reporting standards; send only risk-flagged cases to USCIS. Publish processing benchmarks aligned to academic calendars and ensure continuation of study and on-campus work until adjudication.

Phased transition with empirical checkpoints. If proceeding, pilot the framework with clear metrics (fraud detection, overstay rates, processing performance) and adjust based on results.

Conclusion
Because the NPRM does not demonstrate a least-burdensome approach, adequately address small-entity impacts, or reconcile foreseeable processing and compliance harms with documented benefits, it should be withdrawn or substantially revised. A calibrated framework—preserving D/S with strengthened SEVIS validations and deploying USCIS adjudication only where indicated by risk—would better meet oversight goals while safeguarding program feasibility, due process, and the integrity of U.S. higher education.

The rule would delete the current regulatory deference to prior USCIS determinations for cases involving the same parties and the same underlying facts, and replace it with a broad statement that extensions “may be granted at USCIS’s discretion,” while reiterating that denials are not appealable. At minimum, pair any change with transparent service-level goals, a robust motion-to-reopen/reconsider pathway, and explicit language that prior approvals are not unsettled absent the enumerated exceptions.

Request: Withdraw the proposed rule in its entirety.

Summary
International students, exchange visitors, and foreign media representatives are already subject to extensive monitoring through SEVIS and other DHS systems, and research consistently shows that immigrants—including these groups—have significantly lower crime and violation rates than the U.S.-born population. The proposal offers no credible evidence or quantified security gains to justify replacing “duration of status” (D/S) with fixed admission periods. Instead, it would add recurring bureaucracy, disrupt graduate-level research programs, and undermine U.S. competitiveness in attracting global talent.

1. Public-safety rationale is unsupported.
Immigrants, including international students, already have far lower crime rates than natives. An NBER study shows immigrants are about 60% less likely to be incarcerated than the U.S.-born, a trend consistent across 150 years. Texas records show legal immigrants—the group that includes F/J holders—have the lowest conviction rates. Reviews by Reuters and others conclude claims of disproportionate immigrant crime are unfounded. The NPRM does not explain how fixed terms improve safety.

2. Compliance concerns are already addressed.
International students are continuously monitored through SEVIS. DHS Entry/Exit Overstay Reports show suspected student overstay rates are low and decline as departures are confirmed. These are administrative, not criminal issues. No evidence shows replacing D/S with fixed terms would improve compliance.

3. XXXXX to U.S. research and competitiveness.
Temporary-visa holders earn a large share of America’s advanced degrees: NSF reports ~35% of S&E doctorates and ~34% of all doctorates in 2023 went to temporary residents. About 73% of foreign S&E PhDs stay in the U.S. a decade after graduation, driving patents, innovation, and spillovers to U.S. collaborators. Forcing serial extensions mid-PhD will deter enrollment and push talent abroad.

4. Design choices disrupt graduate education.
The rule would:
• Limit admission to four years;
• XXXXX F-1 graduate program changes mid-course;
• Require a year at the initial school before transfer;
• Cut the grace period from 60 to 30 days;
• Require biometrics for each extension.
These provisions interfere with normal academic decisions and research cycles, creating avoidable risks for programs that often last 5–7 years.

5. Costs outweigh benefits.
DHS itself projects ≈205,000 F and 203,000 J extension filings annually, with $86–88 million in annualized costs. These burdens fall on students, schools, and USCIS without quantified security gains.

6. The proposal ignores reliance interests and history.
A nearly identical rule in 2020 was withdrawn in 2021 after widespread opposition. XXXXX built around D/S should not face renewed disruption without new justification.

Recommendation:
Withdraw the NPRM. At minimum, DHS should:

1.Retain D/S for graduate research programs;
2.Allow program changes and restore the 60-day grace period;
3.Avoid duplicative biometrics;
4.Demonstrate evidence of net safety gains.

Conclusion:
International students are among the most law-abiding populations in the U.S. They are vital to American research leadership and economic strength. This rule addresses no real safety problem while predictably harming higher education and innovation. DHS should withdraw it.
