I am writing to express my concerns regarding the proposed rule that seeks to establish a fixed maximum period of admission for F, J, and I visa holders. While I fully understand and respect the government's legitimate interest in strengthening national security and improving oversight of nonimmigrant visa holders, I believe that, in its current form, this proposal may have unintended negative consequences for thousands of international students and scholars who are fully compliant with U.S. immigration law. I would like to offer the following two main points:

First, I agree that national security is an essential component of immigration policy and that continued attention and improvement in this area is both necessary and appropriate. However, any reforms intended to enhance national security should be evidence-based, narrowly tailored, and avoid overgeneralization. The current proposal applies sweeping restrictions to all academic students and exchange visitors—regardless of their individual compliance history or risk level. The vast majority of these individuals are law-abiding, contribute significantly to U.S. educational institutions, and do not pose a threat to national security.

Rather than imposing a blanket four-year (or in some cases, two-year) limit on the admission period for all students, it would be more effective to focus on identifying specific risk factors associated with potential visa misuse. For example, the government could strengthen interagency information sharing, implement targeted monitoring measures, or establish individualized review mechanisms. XXXXX policies that penalize compliant students undermine trust in the immigration system and place unnecessary burdens on those who contribute meaningfully to U.S. academic and research communities.

Second, the proposed four-year limit is particularly impractical for doctoral students. The majority of Ph.D. programs in the United States take five years or more to complete. Imposing a four-year limit would force nearly all international doctoral students to apply for an extension during their studies, which introduces unnecessary bureaucratic delays, financial costs, and uncertainty. In many cases, students would need to leave the U.S. to renew their visas abroad, incurring travel expenses, disrupting research timelines, and potentially facing visa processing delays that impact their ability to return.

Such instability may interfere with academic progress and mental well-being, while offering little to no added benefit in terms of national security. These students are not only future researchers and innovators but also essential participants in the day-to-day operations of U.S. higher education. Policy changes should be designed to ensure both their compliance and their ability to succeed in their academic goals.

Additionally, I believe this proposal could have broader implications for the development of diversity within American society. The United States is a deeply diverse country, and it requires a workforce that reflects and supports that diversity. International students and scholars often bring language skills, cultural understanding, and specialized training that enable them to serve communities that are underserved by the domestic workforce. For example, bilingual and multicultural professionals in psychology or social work are critical to providing effective services to immigrant or minority communities. A one-size-fits-all immigration policy could inadvertently limit the presence of such professionals and create downstream social challenges in education, healthcare, and community support systems.

In conclusion, I sincerely hope that the Department of Homeland Security will reconsider the blanket imposition of a fixed admission period for all F and J visa holders. A more nuanced, data-driven approach—one that balances national security with fairness and practicality—would better serve the interests of the United States and its academic institutions, while continuing to welcome those who come here in good faith to study, teach, and contribute.

Comment on Proposed Rule (8 CFR 214.2(f))
Summary
The proposed ban on allowing F-1 students to pursue another program at the same or lower degree
level unfairly harms legitimate students while failing to stop real abuse. The true problem is “Day 1
CPT” PhD programs, where individuals repeatedly enroll not for study but to keep F-1 status and work
full time. This regulation leaves that loophole open, yet blocks genuine students—like PhD holders who
later wish to pursue a JD, MD, PharmD, or MBA. These are distinct, professional programs with unique
purposes, not repetitive academic degrees. PhDs who pursue professional doctorates strengthen
America. A PhD in biology who later trains as an MD or PharmD brings research expertise into U.S.
healthcare, directly benefiting patients and innovation. A PhD who earns a JD learns the U.S. legal
system and carries that knowledge abroad, advancing U.S. values of law and order. International
professional graduates also face steep barriers in the job market and rarely displace American workers.
The proposed rule also contradicts U.S. universities’ own dual-degree pathways—MD-PhD, MD-MPH,
JD-MBA, JD-MPH, and others. If second degrees are broadly prohibited, how can these programs
continue?
Instead of a blanket ban, DHS should:
Distinguish between repetitive academic degrees versus professional or terminal programs with
unique purposes.
Eliminate or tightly restrict “Day 1 CPT.”
• Require at least one academic year of study before CPT eligibility.
• Cap CPT duration at each degree level.
• Strengthen institutional oversight of CPT.
In short, the proposed rule misses its target. It will not stop those who abuse “Day 1 CPT” PhD
programs to keep working, but it will harm students who have always complied with the law and only
seek legitimate education. I urge DHS to refine the rule so it prevents abuse while preserving
opportunities for genuine international students.

Issuing visas with a fixed duration admission period would limit students’ flexibility to pursue academic goals in the United States, reduce U.S. revenue (since the majority of international students pay full tuition costs) and decrease the benefit to U.S. universities and work force of top international talent. According to the National Student Clearinghouse Research Center, of the 1.9 million full-time students who started undergraduate studies in Fall 2016, only 48.8% completed their credential within 4 years. This data shows that a significant percentage of students would be required to extend their status if they were admitted for a 4-year period only, and would risk not being able to complete their degree. This could lead to decreased program completion rates at universities and appeal to foreign populations for recruitment. Requiring an additional EOS application for students who have incurred some kind of medical, academic, or administrative hardship puts an undue burden on students who have already undergone challenges. Instead, allowing a fixed number of DSO permitted extensions prior to requesting a USCIS EOS could allow additional USCIS oversight without imposing a fixed duration admission period.

Hardships for community colleges, English language programs, and preparation programs
The proposed rule creates additional hardships for community colleges, English language programs, or preparation programs who regularly recruit students planning to transfer after completing their program. Creating a fixed admission status would require all of these students to apply for an extension of status, incurring additional costs for these students, and could impact the ability of these students to transfer to appropriate programs. A student who tests at a higher English proficiency level and intends to transfer to a degree program would have to apply for an extension of status immediately and may not receive approval in time to transfer to their desired school. A fixed duration admission status for these students is a hindrance to their pursuit of a U.S. education and a loss to our U.S. educational system of international talent and revenue.

Limiting transfers and change of major in first year of study
Rather than limiting transfer and change of major within the first year, I would request that restrictions on transfer on arrival be addressed specifically. For example, students could be required to study at the school whose SEVIS record they entered on for at least one term.

Even if the student was allowed to transfer in the first year, under the proposed rule, the student would be required to apply twice within a 12 month period for EOS. I oppose this proposal because it solves the wrong problem in the wrong way. The rule assumes that forcing every international student onto a short, fixed clock with recurring extensions will improve integrity. In practice, it will push routine academic life (advisor changes, lab pivots, delayed experiments, and thesis rewrites) through an immigration turnstile that was never designed for that cadence. The students who keep our lecture halls staffed as TAs and our labs running as junior researchers will face status cliffs that have little to do with merit or compliance and everything to do with paperwork timing. Many departments use international enrollment to keep specialized courses open, seed new programs, and fund advising and student services that benefit everyone. When you add uncertainty and friction to that enrollment, small programs cancel sections, hiring freezes spread, and the “choice set” for in-state students narrows. This is not a one-year hit; it compounds as cohorts get thinner and labs postpone projects for lack of stable staffing. In college towns and regional hubs, fewer students and slower research cycles mean emptier apartments, quieter main streets, and less local tax revenue, which is precisely the opposite of what communities want from their public universities.

title: Comment Submitted by Haoran Zhang
comment_clean:
Comment on DHS Proposed XXXXX: “Establishing a Fixed Time Period of Admission and an Extension of XXXXX for Nonimmigrant Academic XXXXX, XXXXX, and Representatives of Foreign Information Media” (RIN 1615-AC66)

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule that would eliminate the long-standing “Duration of XXXXX” (D/S) policy for F, J, and I nonimmigrants and replace it with fixed periods of admission tied to program end dates and maximum limits. While I recognize the Department of Homeland Security’s stated concerns about program oversight and enforcement, I believe this rule is fundamentally misguided and will cause significant harm to the U.S. higher education system, the U.S. economy, and the United States’ reputation as a global leader in education and research.

My objections are as follows:

1. Unreasonable for Long-Term Academic Programs

Doctoral programs in the United States typically take five to seven years to complete, with many students requiring additional time for dissertation research, fieldwork, or unexpected academic delays. A four-year cap on admission is wholly incompatible with this reality and would force the majority of PhD students into an unnecessary and burdensome extension process, often multiple times during their course of study. This undermines the stability and focus required for successful completion of advanced research.

2. Increased Administrative Burden on USCIS and XXXXX

The rule will trigger hundreds of thousands of annual I-539 extension applications. USCIS is already severely backlogged, with processing delays affecting adjustment of status, work authorization, and other critical immigration benefits. Requiring nearly every international student to file multiple extensions will overwhelm an already strained system, delay other immigration petitions, and create uncertainty for students whose research and academic progress depend on uninterrupted lawful presence. The proposal’s reliance on a 240-day grace period during extension adjudication is speculative at best—there is no guarantee USCIS can process such a surge in time.

3. Negative Impact on U.S. Universities, Local XXXXX, and the Economy

International students contribute billions of dollars annually to the U.S. economy and play a vital role in funding universities, particularly through graduate tuition and research assistantships. By reducing the attractiveness of U.S. institutions compared to countries like Canada, the U.K., and Australia—which provide clearer and more supportive student visa pathways—this rule will deter millions of qualified students from applying. The financial impact will be felt not only by universities, but also by domestic students (through higher tuition and fewer program offerings) and by local economies that rely on student spending. Moreover, reducing the international student pool will shrink the pipeline of highly skilled workers and innovators who fuel U.S. competitiveness.

4. Restricting XXXXX is Counterproductive

The proposed ban on pursuing a second degree at the same academic level is arbitrary and fails to reflect the realities of today’s knowledge economy. For example, a student who has completed an MBA program may wish to pursue a master’s in artificial intelligence to better integrate technical and managerial decision-making in industries increasingly shaped by large language models (LLMs). Preventing such cross-disciplinary study deprives the U.S. of the kind of agile, adaptive workforce needed in the 21st century.

5. XXXXX Regulation That Fails to Address XXXXX

The proposal frames D/S as an enforcement challenge, but there are targeted alternatives that would more effectively address compliance without penalizing millions of law-abiding students. Improved SEVIS reporting, better coordination with academic institutions, and stricter oversight of programs prone to abuse (e.g., misuse of Day 1 CPT) would directly address the stated concerns. Instead, this rule imposes a blanket restriction that punishes legitimate students and programs for the misconduct of a minority.

Conclusion
The proposed rule undermines the very strengths that make the United States a global destination for education and research: flexibility, academic excellence, and a welcoming environment for the world’s brightest minds. It will overburden USCIS, harm universities and local economies, reduce America’s competitiveness, and deter future generations of international students. For these reasons, I strongly urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and instead pursue narrower, evidence-based reforms that address specific compliance issues without imposing widespread harm.

The statutory F-1 definition, INA § 101(a)(15)(F) (8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(15)(F)), does not impose a categorical bar on same-level study. DHS already regulates academic progression through 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(f) and SEVIS/DSO oversight (transfer/change-of-level rules) to ensure a bona fide full course of study and proper maintenance of status. A new blanket ban is unnecessary.

B. Overbroad relative to DHS’s stated concern
DHS cites patterns of “program-hopping” and proposes several related controls. But those concerns can be addressed case-by-case with SEVIS analytics, targeted DSO scrutiny, and existing transfer/change-of-objective procedures—without banning legitimate same-level second degrees outright. The categorical bar in (f)(5)(ii)(C) sweeps in bona fide reskilling paths (e.g., software engineering → statistics/data science) that clearly advance academic and workforce goals.

C. XXXXX and workforce downsides
International students are vital to U.S. higher education and the STEM workforce. Authoritative sources show they contributed ~$43.8B and ~378,000 jobs in 2023/24, while foreign-born workers comprise ~19% of the U.S. STEM workforce. Curbing legitimate second-degree pathways would chill needed re/up-skilling and reduce positive spillovers to universities and local economies.(https://www.nafsa.org/about/about-nafsa/international-students-contribute-record-breaking-level-spending-and-378000-jobs)

D. APA concerns: failure to weigh reliance interests and less-restrictive options
For decades, DHS has allowed supervised changes of educational level and transfers within the existing framework. Abruptly replacing that with a categorical ban—without robust consideration of reliance interests of students, schools, and employers—risks an arbitrary and capricious outcome under the APA. See DHS v. Regents of the Univ. of California (2020) (agency must consider reliance interests). Supreme Court(https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/19pdf/18-587_5ifl.pdf)

E. The proposal’s own framework favors individualized review
The rule elsewhere leans on a student’s educational/professional objective as a compliance metric. That logic supports individualized review rather than a categorical prohibition. Allowing same-level programs when a school’s DSO documents a good-faith educational rationale (reskilling, upskilling, interdisciplinary study, or academic progression) would deter abuse without harming bona fide cases.

3) Personal impact (experience)
I am a foreign professional in the U.S. on a valid work visa and plan to pursue a second master’s degree to retool for evolving industry needs. Under proposed § 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(C), I would be barred from changing to F-1 for a same-level program pursued in good faith for career progression—foreclosing a critical pathway that benefits U.S. universities and employers.

4) Proposed alternative
Replace proposed § 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(C) with:
(C) An alien who has completed a program in the United States as an F-1 nonimmigrant at one educational level may commence another program at the same educational level if the Designated School Official (DSO) certifies in SEVIS that the new program has a good-faith educational rationale (including reskilling, upskilling, interdisciplinary study, or academic progression). DHS may request additional information and may deny eligibility upon a specific, individualized finding of abuse.
Optional guardrails, if DHS insists: 
• Reasonable limits on repeated same-level programs absent exceptional circumstances; 
• A short DSO note describing the rationale (e.g., reskilling or added competencies); 
• No change to existing OPT structure (no “extra” same-level OPT beyond current rules).

title: MM37 Comment Submitted by Christine Bratton
comment_clean:
I am writing to urge the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw its August 28, 2025 proposal to limit the duration of visas for foreign journalists in the United States.

These changes would harm press freedom and American interests more broadly by introducing the following unnecessary barriers and serious risks:
Excessive administrative burden and uncertainty: Requiring frequent renewals every few months would distract journalists from their core work, and create anxiety about whether the visas they rely on for their livelihood will be renewed.

Chilling effect on press freedom: Continuous scrutiny by government officials on an individual exercising their constitutional right to free speech, especially with the life-altering consequences of denying a visa based on an officer’s broad discretion, could lead to self-censorship and severely inhibit the freedom of the press in the US.

Potential abuse: The new visa restrictions will leave journalists wondering if their visas will be cancelled because a single bureaucrat disapproved of the content of their journalism.

Diminishing the standing of the United States abroad: Billions of people around the world, speaking thousands of languages, rely daily on journalists who understand their culture, as well as the context in the US. The absence of this reporting will diminish the standing of the United States while empowering its potential adversaries to fill gaps in reporting.

Empowering authoritarian censors abroad: Requiring a journalist to be a representative of a foreign media organization will disproportionately harm independent journalists from repressive countries like Iran, Venezuela, and Russia, who are likely to not have a formal relationship with media in the country and more likely to face repression if expelled from the US.
Given these self-defeating and concerning consequences, I strongly urge the Department of Homeland Security to abandon this proposal. Preserving freedom of speech and of the press by allowing law-abiding journalists to tell America’s story to their global audience makes America stronger and helps us live up to our founding principles.

Thank you for your attention to this critical matter.

proposed rule that would impose a maximum two-year enrollment limit on English as a Second
Language (ESL) programs for F visa holders, as well as replace the current “duration of status”
system with fixed admission periods.
1. Two-Year ESL Cap Is Unrealistic and XXXXX
Language acquisition is a complex and deeply individual process. The proposal to cap ESL
enrollment at two years fails to recognize the wide variation in students’ starting levels, learning
pace, and long-term goals. Many adult learners—especially those beginning at low
proficiency—require more than two years to reach college-level fluency or to function effectively
in a professional or academic environment. Imposing an arbitrary two-year limit will prevent
committed, law-abiding students from completing their programs, forcing them to abandon their
goals or navigate unnecessary and costly visa changes.
2. Negative Impact on U.S. ESL Schools, XXXXX, and XXXXX
ESL schools across the United States—many of which are private institutions—depend heavily
on F visa students for enrollment and tuition revenue. These schools not only serve students but
also employ thousands of American citizens as teachers, administrators, and support
staff. The proposed cap would significantly reduce student numbers, leading to program
downsizing or closures. This would result in direct job losses and negatively affect local
economies, particularly in states and cities that host a high concentration of ESL programs.
In addition, the economic contributions of F visa holders—through housing, transportation, food,
entertainment, and more—extend well beyond the classroom. Curtailing ESL study periods
would ripple through local businesses and state economies, undermining the very communities
that benefit from international education.

international students to focus on their education without fear of arbitrary deadlines. Switching to
a fixed-period admission—even with the possibility of extensions—adds administrative burden,
legal uncertainty, and anxiety for students and institutions alike. It also increases the workload
for USCIS, which is already backlogged, and creates unnecessary risk of status violations due
to processing delays.
Conclusion: Withdraw the ESL Cap and Preserve D/S Admission

create systemic harm to international students, U.S. schools, American workers, and local

 Remove the proposed 2-year cap on ESL programs.

title: Comment Submitted by S B
comment_clean:
First, I’d like to sincerely thank USCIS for taking the initiative to revisit and modernize student visa regulations. These efforts reflect a meaningful commitment to strengthening the U.S. higher education system and reaffirming America’s leadership in global student enrollment. I’m confident that the final rules will aim to support the aspirations of American universities, the economy, and the students who choose to study here.
By way of introduction, I am an international student currently on an F-1 visa. I have successfully completed my academic program, completed my period of Optional Practical Training (OPT), and am presently in the STEM OPT extension phase. My journey through the U.S. education and immigration system has given me firsthand insight into the challenges and opportunities faced by students navigating these transitions.
While I’m encouraged by the direction of these reforms, I’d like to share a few thoughts on how certain provisions might be refined to better serve both international students and the broader goals of the U.S. education and workforce systems.
1. Academic Year Requirement Before Transfer or Change of Program
Proposed XXXXX: 8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(i)(D)
This provision may benefit from added flexibility. International students often make significant personal and financial commitments to study in the U.S., and it’s not uncommon—especially in the first semester—for them to discover that their initial academic path isn’t the right fit. This happens with domestic students as well. Whether due to a mismatch in learning style, career goals, or program focus, students may find that a change is necessary to stay on track academically and professionally.
Requiring students to remain for a full academic year in a program that doesn’t align with their goals may unintentionally create added stress and uncertainty. For many, the first semester is a time of adjustment—academically, culturally, and personally. If they quickly realize that their chosen program isn’t the right fit, being locked into it for an entire year could lead to unnecessary financial strain and delay their progress. This kind of rigidity can discourage students from continuing their education in the U.S. or from recommending American institutions to future applicants abroad. When students are empowered to make timely, thoughtful changes to their academic path, they’re more likely to thrive—and that benefits not just the individual, but the institutions they attend and the workforce they eventually join.
The current system already ensures program integrity by requiring students to maintain status and transfer only to SEVP-certified institutions. A more flexible approach—especially in the early stages of study—could help students make timely, beneficial adjustments without compromising oversight.
Suggested Adjustment: Consider expanding the list of exceptions to include academic mismatch, financial hardship, program closure, or personal well-being. This would allow students to make informed changes when needed, while still upholding the integrity of the visa process.
Conclusion: A rigid one-year lock-in period creates unnecessary stress and financial burden, discourages timely academic adjustment, and risks reducing the appeal of U.S. higher education. Allowing earlier transfers under defined exceptions would preserve integrity while supporting student success.

To Whom It May Concern:

I strongly oppose DHS’s proposed rule to end “Duration of XXXXX” (D/S) and replace it with a fixed admission period for F and J visa holders. This change is unnecessary, harmful, and counterproductive for the following reasons:

1. Unnecessary Bureaucracy and Increased USCIS Backlogs
Requiring hundreds of thousands of students and exchange visitors to file Form I-539 extensions every few years will overwhelm USCIS. DHS itself projects annualized costs approaching $390 million over 10 years. Instead of improving compliance, this rule drains adjudication resources from high-risk cases, worsens the backlog, and multiplies RFEs and appeals—none of which improve security. In short, it institutionalizes unnecessary bureaucracy, USCIS backlog, and inefficiency.

2. XXXXX to U.S. Higher Education and XXXXX
International students contribute tens of billions of dollars each year in tuition and local spending, sustaining U.S. universities and creating American jobs. Over 1.6 million F-1 admissions occurred in FY 2023—a major pillar of U.S. higher education. Immigration uncertainty will drive top talent to Canada, the UK, Australia, and Singapore, harming U.S. universities’ budgets, local businesses, and America’s global competitiveness for talent.

3. Disproportionate Punishment and “Identity Trap”
Cutting the grace period from 60 to 30 days and imposing frequent renewals exposes students to harsh penalties for minor technical violations. A simple paperwork delay can cause lawful students to accrue unlawful presence, jeopardizing visas or careers. These unnecessary hardships do not improve security but disproportionately punish legitimate students and researchers.

4. National Security and Foreign Policy Backfire
Overregulation discourages high-value international talent from choosing the U.S., weakening our leadership in science, technology, and innovation. If enacted, this rule will shrink the pipeline of skilled researchers and professionals, undermining America’s technological and security edge while benefiting competitor nations.

5. Better Alternatives Exist
DHS already runs SEVIS—a robust real-time monitoring system managed by Designated School Officials (DSOs) and Responsible Officers (ROs). This gives the government oversight without mass extension filings. Rather than reverting to a pre-1979 model abandoned for inefficiency, DHS should enhance SEVIS analytics and target actual fraud.

Conclusion
This proposed rule will not meaningfully improve compliance or security. Instead, it creates unnecessary bureaucracy, exacerbates USCIS backlog, harms higher education and the economy, and undermines America’s competitive edge. I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule and retain the proven “Duration of XXXXX” framework for F and J visa holders.

Respectfully submitted,
Anonymous Commenter

I strongly oppose the proposal to eliminate “duration of status” (D/S) and replace it with fixed admission periods for F, J, and I nonimmigrants. My own experience during the COVID-19 pandemic illustrates how unpredictable events can make fixed timelines unworkable.

1. Disruption to XXXXX and Practical Training
The rule proposes limiting admission periods for F-1 students to a maximum of four years, with separate extension applications required for longer study or work authorization (Proposed XXXXX, p. 53, §214.2(f)). During the COVID-19 pandemic, travel was unsafe and, in many cases, impossible. Students with valid programs and authorization had no practical way to leave the U.S. or re-enter safely. A rigid fixed-time system would have left many students unlawfully present through no fault of their own. Duration of status provided essential flexibility to navigate crises without risking sudden loss of lawful presence. Replacing it with hard end-dates ignores these real-world contingencies and exposes students to penalties for circumstances outside their control.

DHS estimates that the rule will impose annualized costs of up to $392 million over ten years, including fees and paperwork burdens on students, schools, and exchange sponsors (Proposed XXXXX, p. 70, Cost-Benefit Summary). Retain duration of status for F, J, and I nonimmigrants, coupled with targeted reviews of SEVIS compliance.

I respectfully oppose the Department of Homeland Security’s proposed rule to replace “duration of status” (D/S) with fixed admission periods for F, J, and I nonimmigrants. As an individual commenter, I believe this rule would create excessive costs, disrupt academic and exchange programs, and reduce U.S. competitiveness in higher education without sufficient evidence that the change would improve compliance or security (Proposed XXXXX, pp. 27–32, §III).

1. Administrative and Financial Burdens
DHS itself estimates annualized costs of $390–392 million across affected parties, including $86–88 million for U.S. schools and program sponsors (Proposed XXXXX, p. 104, §IV.C). These costs reflect filing fees, staff time, and compliance burdens. Many universities already devote significant resources to SEVIS reporting. Adding mandatory extension applications would overwhelm Designated School Officials (DSOs) and Responsible Officers (ROs), diverting resources from academic support to paperwork.
Example: A large university hosting several thousand international students would face hundreds of new extension filings each year, requiring additional staff and raising the risk of processing delays.

2. XXXXX and XXXXX
The rule would limit F-1 admission and extensions to no more than four years and restrict program changes and transfers (Proposed XXXXX, pp. 73–75, §214.2 amendments). It also reduces the post-completion grace period from 60 to 30 days (Proposed XXXXX, p. 77, §214.2(f)(5)(iv)). These restrictions disproportionately harm students and scholars in longer programs, or those facing legitimate delays.
Example: A Ph.D. student in engineering often requires five to six years to complete research. Forcing a mid-program extension introduces uncertainty that jeopardizes grant-funded projects and dissertation timelines.
Example: A student who takes medical leave may be unable to obtain an extension under the narrowed criteria, leading to loss of legal status through no fault of their own.

3. Weak Justification for Eliminating D/S
The proposal argues that D/S creates risks of overstays and fraud (Proposed XXXXX, pp. 35–41, §III.A). However, DHS already monitors compliance through SEVIS, which provides real-time reporting on status, transfers, and violations. The rule does not present compelling evidence that D/S has failed, nor that fixed admission periods would solve the cited problems. Instead, it risks punishing the overwhelming majority of compliant students, scholars, and journalists for the actions of a small minority.

Practical Alternatives
Rather than eliminate D/S entirely, DHS could:

Retain D/S while strengthening targeted SEVIS-based compliance reviews.

Provide a safe harbor for individuals with timely-filed extension requests to prevent accrual of unlawful presence due to processing delays.

Establish clear, transparent criteria for program extensions, giving both students and institutions predictability while preserving flexibility.

Conclusion
The proposed rule would impose high costs, administrative burdens, and academic disruption while offering limited security benefits. Maintaining D/S with enhanced compliance checks would better balance enforcement with America’s longstanding commitment to educational and cultural exchange.

Respectfully submitted

I respectfully oppose DHS’s proposal to eliminate “duration of status” (D/S) for F, J, and I nonimmigrants and replace it with fixed admission periods. While the stated goal is to improve oversight, the rule lacks data to justify such a sweeping change and would impose significant administrative costs and academic disruptions. More targeted adjustments, rather than a wholesale replacement of D/S, would better achieve DHS’s objectives.

1. Administrative and Cost Burdens
The rule itself estimates annualized costs of $390–392 million, with $86–88 million borne by U.S. institutions and program sponsors (Proposed XXXXX, p. 104, §IV.C).

Substantive Concern: DHS has not provided a granular breakdown of how these costs were calculated, such as staff hours per extension, or the expected number of filings per school. Without such detail, it is impossible to evaluate whether the rule is cost-effective.

Recommendation: Instead of requiring universal extensions, DHS could leverage SEVIS for targeted audits of outlier cases, which would conserve resources while maintaining oversight.

2. Risks to XXXXX
The rule caps F-1 admission and extensions at four years and cuts the grace period after completion from 60 to 30 days (Proposed XXXXX, pp. 73–77, §214.2 amendments).

Substantive Concern: STEM doctoral programs in the U.S. often last five to six years, as shown by National Science Foundation data. A four-year cap is fundamentally misaligned with actual degree lengths, guaranteeing widespread extension filings.

Example: A Ph.D. student whose research is delayed by lab equipment failure may not qualify for an extension, since the rule deems “academic delays” an unacceptable reason (Proposed XXXXX, p. 75). This would unfairly jeopardize the student’s legal status.

Recommendation: DHS should create longer authorized admission periods—such as six years—for doctoral and research programs to match academic realities.

3. Lack of Evidence that D/S Fails
The proposal asserts that D/S undermines enforcement of overstay rules and creates fraud incentives (Proposed XXXXX, pp. 35–41, §III.A). Yet it provides no clear data on:

The actual percentage of F/J/I overstays under D/S,

How often SEVIS fails to detect status violations, or

Why existing enforcement mechanisms are insufficient.

Substantive Concern: Without such evidence, eliminating D/S for millions of compliant nonimmigrants lacks justification.

Recommendation: DHS should publish disaggregated data on D/S-related overstays and compliance gaps before finalizing any rule, to demonstrate necessity.

4. Practical Alternatives
Rather than abolishing D/S entirely, DHS could adopt a more balanced approach:

Retain D/S while using SEVIS to flag and review high-risk cases (e.g., unusually long enrollments, repeated transfers).

Define clear and transparent criteria for extensions, explicitly allowing for medical leave, research delays, and force majeure events (such as pandemics).

Provide a safe harbor: if a nonimmigrant timely files an extension, their status and work authorization should automatically continue until adjudication is complete.

Conclusion
This proposal would impose heavy costs and academic disruption while offering only speculative security benefits. Maintaining D/S, paired with strengthened SEVIS-based oversight and tailored safeguards, would strike a better balance between enforcement and America’s long-standing role as a global leader in education and cultural exchange.

Respectfully submitted,

The proposed shift risks driving away highly skilled students and exchange visitors who often remain in the U.S. workforce through Optional Practical Training (OPT) and later as employees of U.S. firms. Luna

title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comment_clean:
I am a PhD student who collaborates closely with international students and scholars. These students and scholars make immeasurable contributions to the United States economy and society, in the face of continuing challenges due to their immigration status. I am writing to urge the Department of Homeland Security not to implement the proposed changes to 8 CFR, and to maintain the current Duration of Status framework.

The proposed introduction of specific departure dates for F, I, and J nonimmigrants in XXXXX. ICEB-2XXXXX is overwhelmingly likely to reduce the number and quality of international students and scholars applying for visas for legitimate reasons and within complete compliance with the rules. The proposed changes include setting the authorized admission and extension periods for F and J nonimmigrants up to the program length, not to exceed a 4-year period, with the additional note that a delay in completing one's program generally is an unacceptable reason for program extensions for F nonimmigrants. Particularly in the case of PhD students, and many combined undergraduate-graduate programs, these restrictions are completely unreasonable. PhD programs have an average duration well over 4 years. In my program, many students (US citizens and international) whose PhDs were interrupted by the covid-19 pandemic have taken much longer than 5 years to complete their research through no fault of their own. Program lengths also vary substantially by research area, so some areas of American scholarship will be especially harmed by the changes. Under these proposed changes, future international students and scholars will be unable to complete a PhD without requesting a visa extension and paying its associated costs. If these visa extensions are denied, students face the loss of years of progress. In light of the unreasonably difficult hurdles these changes place in the path of international students intending to complete PhDs in the US, international students will choose not to come to the US at all - particularly the best and brightest potential students, whose valuable skills will enable them to find positions elsewhere.

The proposed restrictions on program changes under XXXXX. ICEB-2XXXXX are also excessively harmful. These changes will prevent graduate students from changing programs at any point during their program of study, a restriction which is entirely impractical. When my PhD supervisor moved institution, some of her PhD students likewise transferred institutions to remain with her. Under these new rules, this option would be unavailable to international students. I am also aware of situations in which graduate students have been harassed by other people at their original institution, and as a result have had to move to another institution for their safety. International graduate students, like all graduate students, should have the right to move for their safety without jeopardizing their degree progress or their immigration status. These draconian new restrictions will result in international graduate students being forced to lose progress towards their degrees due to circumstances outside of their control.

Further, the proposed changes in XXXXX. ICEB-2XXXXX are harmful to Americans. International students coming to universities in the US contribute billions of dollars to the US economy. When many more choose to go to other countries due to these proposals, the economic growth of the US will suffer. Many universities are able to subsidize the education of American students using the tuition money paid by international students, and American students gain both cultural and technical knowledge from interacting with their international peers. The research conducted by international students and scholars is also an enormous driver of US innovation. Without international students and scholars who choose to come to the US under the F, J, and I nonimmigrant visa programs, US citizens will live in a poorer and less culturally rich nation.

And all of these changes are entirely unnecessary. While DHS claims to have identified over 2,100 aliens who have maintained F-1 status for over 15 years, this represents a miniscule percentage of the number of students on F visas in the United States. The United States has existing legislation to combat fake educational institutions, aka visa mills, already ensuring that students in the US are engaged in legitimate study. The proposed rule changes will harm international students and scholars coming to the US for legitimate purposes of study, rather than catching people coming to the US under false pretenses.

For the wellbeing of international students, the integrity of US higher education, and the nation's continued leadership in research and innovation, I urge the DHS to reject these proposed changes and preserve the current Duration of XXXXX.

Comment Opposing Proposed XXXXX on XXXXX for F, J, and I Nonimmigrants (DHS Docket No. ICEB-2XXXXX)

Executive Summary
I respectfully oppose the proposed rule to replace “duration of status” (D/S) with fixed admission periods for F academic students, J exchange visitors, and I foreign media representatives (Proposed XXXXX PDF, pp. 33–37, §214.2). While intended to increase oversight, the proposal risks imposing severe, unintended harms on students who face unforeseen health, academic, or personal emergencies. A rigid system would add layers of bureaucratic stress at moments when individuals are already most vulnerable.

1. XXXXX
During my time in the United States on an F-1 visa, I was diagnosed with a serious medical condition. Like anyone in such a situation, I needed time to prioritize treatment and recovery before resuming full academic progress. Under the current D/S system, Designated School Officials (DSOs) can grant appropriate program extensions (Proposed XXXXX PDF, p. 78, §214.2(f)(7)(iii)). This flexibility allowed me to remain in compliance while managing my health responsibly.

Under the proposed fixed admission model, a student in my position would be forced not only to battle a life-altering diagnosis but also the stress and uncertainty of filing for an extension of stay (EOS) with USCIS. This process is costly, time-consuming, and may not align with the unpredictable timelines of medical treatment. The rule specifically limits acceptable reasons for program extensions, stating that delays due to probation, suspension, or repeated inability to complete studies are “generally unacceptable” (Proposed XXXXX PDF, p. 131, §214.2(f)(7)(v)). This narrow framing could leave students with legitimate health crises unfairly vulnerable to status loss.

2. XXXXX on Students and XXXXX
DHS estimates annualized costs of up to $392 million from this rule (Proposed XXXXX PDF, p. 168, Summary of Costs). For students facing health emergencies, these costs are not abstract—they represent real financial and emotional strain. Filing an EOS during illness requires gathering documentation, paying fees, and navigating complex procedures, diverting critical time and resources from recovery and education. For schools, additional reporting and advising duties would compound existing workloads, weakening their ability to provide individualized student support.

3. Risk of Unlawful Presence and Deportation
The rule warns that students who overstay due to unforeseen delays will begin accruing unlawful presence, triggering harsh immigration penalties (Proposed XXXXX PDF, p. 59, §212(a)(9)(B)(i)). For someone facing a serious medical diagnosis, this means that a delay outside their control could cascade into life-changing immigration consequences—barriers to returning to the U.S., loss of academic investment, and even separation from necessary medical care.

Practical Alternatives
•Retain D/S with targeted reviews: Instead of eliminating D/S, DHS could strengthen SEVIS reporting or introduce periodic check-ins for higher-risk categories while preserving flexibility for legitimate emergencies.
•Safe harbor during medical crises: Explicitly provide that students with documented health conditions receive automatic protection from unlawful presence accrual while extensions are pending.
•Streamlined medical EOS: Create a fast-track, low-cost process for extensions based on serious illness, similar to existing humanitarian relief frameworks.

Conclusion
This rule’s rigid approach fails to account for real-world challenges that students face, especially during medical emergencies. A balanced policy should safeguard program integrity while ensuring that serious illness does not also become a basis for loss of lawful status. I urge DHS to withdraw or substantially revise this proposal to retain D/S or provide clear protections for students in crisis.

I strongly oppose DHS’s proposal to replace “duration of status” (D/S) with fixed admission periods for F, J, and I nonimmigrants. This rule will cause significant and lasting harm to U.S. higher education, scientific innovation, and America’s global competitiveness.

Re: DHS RIN 1653-AA95; XXXXX ICEB-2XXXXX — “Establishing a Fixed Time Period of Admission and an Extension of XXXXX for Nonimmigrant Academic Students, XXXXX, and Representatives of Foreign Information Media” (90 FR 42070, Aug. 28, 2025)

Summary. Please revise the NPRM. Replacing D/S with a fixed admission period of up to four years for F and J, cutting F-1’s grace period to 30 days, and routing status continuity through USCIS EOS will create large, recurring burdens without proportionate, evidence-based benefits.

1) Costs and workload. DHS’s RIA estimates annualized costs of $390.3–$392.4 million for all parties and $86.3–$88.1 million for U.S. parties over 10 years. DHS projects average annual EOS volumes of 205,000 (F), 203,000 (J), and 6,000 (I). These volumes will strain adjudications and school sponsors, especially at academic peaks, with no quantified enforcement gain. [90 FR 42070, printed pp. 42074, 42101–42103]

2) XXXXX and implementation risk. SEVP reports 1,582,808 active F-1/M-1 student records in 2024 (+5.3% YoY). Even a modest share needing EOS yields substantial caseflow and raises lapse risk from timing variability. [SEVIS by the Numbers 2024]

3) Unlawful-presence exposure and travel friction. With a fixed I-94 end date, nonimmigrants begin accruing unlawful presence after expiration absent timely approval/tolling, with serious effects on study, OPT/AT, and future admissions. Reducing F-1’s grace period from 60 to 30 days tightens already compressed timelines for wrap-up, transfers, or error correction. [90 FR 42070]

4) U.S. competitiveness. International students and exchange visitors contributed $43.8B and supported 378,175 U.S. jobs in AY 2023–24. Added friction that depresses enrollment risks material economic losses. [NAFSA XXXXX]

5) Targeted, lower-burden alternatives.
• Retain D/S with strengthened SEVIS oversight: risk-based analytics, random audits, and verified DSO/RO attestations tied to annual SEVIS validations, instead of blanket EOS filings.
• If fixing admission, set F-1 to program end date or ≥6 years and authorize automatic continuation of status upon timely DSO SEVIS certification while USCIS processes EOS, mirroring existing employment-authorization continuation constructs.
• Preserve the 60-day F-1 grace period to reduce inadvertent violations and support orderly OPT/Cap-Gap, transfers, and departures.
• Codify student-centric tolling and travel rules so lawful presence continues during timely, non-frivolous EOS pendency and inter-agency timing mismatches do not cause penalties.

(a) Amend 8 CFR 214.2(f)/(j) to require annual DSO/RO SEVIS recertification with DHS audit authority, in lieu of striking D/S.
(b) Where fixed admission is retained, cap at “program end date or six (6) years, whichever is sooner” for F-1; retain the 60-day grace period at 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(iv).
(c) Add a status-continuation clause deeming F/J status unexpired during timely-filed EOS pendency upon SEVIS attestation.

Conclusion. The draft framework shifts large costs and risks to students, schools, sponsors, and USCIS without a proportionate showing of net benefits. DHS can meet oversight goals through enhanced SEVIS validation, audit authority, clear continuation/tolling rules, and by retaining the 60-day F-1 grace period.

title: Comment Submitted by Roger Yan
comment_clean:
I respectfully submit this comment regarding the proposed rule “Establishing a Fixed Time Period of Admission and an Extension of XXXXX for Nonimmigrant XXXXX Students, XXXXX, and Representatives of Foreign Information Media” (Docket No. ICEB-2XXXXX). While the stated intent of strengthening program oversight is understandable, the proposal to eliminate “duration of status” (D/S) and impose fixed admission periods for F-1 students raises serious concerns about administrative feasibility, regulatory proportionality, and the long-term competitiveness of U.S. higher education.

The proposed shift from D/S to fixed admission periods would generate an unprecedented administrative burden for both students and federal agencies. Under the current system, schools and the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) can focus resources on substantive compliance and risk-based enforcement rather than on arbitrary expiration dates. By contrast, the proposed regime would require hundreds of thousands of additional extension-of-stay (EOS) applications annually. Many academic programs—particularly doctoral, dual-degree, and research-intensive pathways—routinely exceed four years, and even shorter programs may extend due to legitimate academic, medical, or personal reasons. Each additional filing carries legal costs, prolonged processing times, and the risk of denial. Any administrative delay could inadvertently trigger unlawful presence, even where students have fully complied. This regulatory uncertainty would likely deter highly qualified international students and complicate institutional enrollment planning.

Equally concerning are the proposed restrictions on changing majors, transferring institutions, or pursuing second degrees. XXXXX mobility and intellectual exploration are integral to U.S. higher education and contribute directly to innovation and research excellence. Restricting program changes during the first year or prohibiting second degrees at the same or lower level would not target bad actors but would instead constrain legitimate academic development. Such inflexibility undermines academic freedom, threatens student well-being, and could dissuade talented students from choosing U.S. institutions, particularly when competitor countries maintain more adaptive frameworks.

The proposal to shorten the post-completion grace period from 60 days to 30 days would further compound these challenges. Thirty days is often insufficient for students to arrange departure, secure new status, or transition to employment—especially amid financial, logistical, or health-related constraints. XXXXX departures increase the likelihood of inadvertent overstays, creating additional enforcement workload without advancing security objectives.

In addition, the proposed rule raises concerns under the Administrative Procedure Act by disrupting the reliance interests of students who entered under the existing D/S framework. DHS has not provided sufficiently disaggregated data demonstrating that D/S has caused widespread abuse or that the benefits of fixed admission periods outweigh their considerable costs. International students contribute over $40 billion annually to the U.S. economy, bolster the nation’s research capacity, and foster global networks that advance U.S. strategic interests. Curtailing their ability to study flexibly would weaken America’s position relative to competitors such as Canada, the United Kingdom, and Australia.

I urge DHS to reconsider the proposed rule and instead pursue a more calibrated approach: retain D/S for longer academic programs, allow reasonable flexibility for program changes and transfers, maintain the 60-day grace period, create safe harbors for timely EOS applicants, and phase in any adjustments based on empirical evidence. Such measures would preserve the integrity of the immigration system while safeguarding the economic, educational, and diplomatic benefits that international students bring to the United States.

As a financial analyst working in workforce planning and corporate forecasting, I have serious concerns with DHS’s proposed rule that eliminates “duration of status” and imposes a fixed four-year limit on F-1 students, while also reducing the grace period from 60 days to 30 days (see p.138 of the proposal).

From a financial planning perspective, these changes create unnecessary uncertainty and volatility in labor force projections. First, international graduates are an integral part of our analyst and associate pipelines. The proposed four-year cap means many PhD or master’s students in quantitative disciplines will be forced to file multiple extensions of stay simply to complete their education. This creates a higher risk of interrupted status, which translates into unpredictable workforce attrition. When companies cannot reliably project headcount, it undermines long-term investment and growth strategies.

Second, reducing the grace period to 30 days introduces a misalignment between immigration rules and real-world financial cycles. Most firms operate on quarterly or annual reporting calendars, and employee transitions are factored into staffing costs, training budgets, and project delivery schedules. A 30-day exit window is simply too short for proper knowledge transfer, final payroll reconciliation, and resource reallocation. This compression increases turnover costs, strains training budgets, and disrupts ongoing client commitments.

Third, DHS itself notes in the proposal that SEVIS already provides real-time oversight of students (p.137). From a risk management standpoint, layering on additional USCIS filings does not materially improve compliance but does significantly increase transaction costs—costs that ultimately get passed along in higher tuition, higher service fees, or reduced competitiveness of U.S. businesses.

Recommendation: DHS should revise the rule to preserve duration of status for F-1 students, especially those in graduate and professional tracks. At a minimum, the 60-day grace period should be retained to align with payroll cycles and workforce transition planning. A rigid 30-day limit is impractical and financially destabilizing for both employers and employees.

For these reasons, I respectfully urge DHS to reconsider and amend this proposal so that it supports, rather than undermines, the financial and human capital stability of U.S. organizations.

title: Comment Submitted by Peter Dye
comment_clean:
To Whom It May Concern,

As a Florida international student advisor, I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule that would impose strict time limits and serious burdens for international students to complete their university degrees or ESL programs and allow “Duration of XXXXX” to remain in effect. This rule would disincentivize international students from coming to the US and would have a devastating effect on our academic institutions. I have worked with international students for my entire professional career, and they are absolutely crucial in making our classrooms and campuses dynamic and distinctive.

The main argument for imposing this rule revolves around protecting national security and preventing visa overstays, but according to DHS’s own report, only 1.15% of international students and exchange visitors overstay their visas. The impact of these students on visa overstay rates is minimal at best, but the impact of losing them from our classrooms, institutions, and communities would be devastating on multiple levels. According to an economic value statistics analysis from NAFSA, nearly 44,767 international students enroll in Florida colleges and universities contributing $1.5 billion to the economy and supporting 12,555 jobs. This data clearly demonstrates international students’ financial contribution to our Florida communities, but their influence goes far beyond just economics.

In pursuing their own academic and professional ambitions, international students wind up improving the educational experiences of the domestic students around them. I have delighted in witnessing my international advisees tutor their native English-speaking peers in different language. I have watched IEP students put their English skills to immediate practical use in their classes for their majors. If one goal of an American university degree is to help form a more well-rounded scholar, professional, and human-being, it would be a tremendous disservice to every student to be surrounded with fewer perspectives and shown a narrower view of the world.

If this ruling takes effect, universities would not be able to offer the same amount of programmatic global learning opportunities on their campuses which further undermines the benefits of international exchange. The amount of time that would be needed to assist students in completing extension-of-stay applications would take a heavy toll on our ability to offer academic programs, intercultural events, peer mentoring, advising appointments, and just about every other thing that our department does well in service of our students. Universities work best when individual students get individual advising related to their academic programs, specific life circumstances, and curricular progress. Faculty advisors and DSOs should be able to continue to evaluate a student’s academic progress and time needed to complete a degree, not the DHS. DHS cannot meet with a student individually. DHS cannot hear about a student’s family member who lost a job or passed away. DHS cannot ask the student if access to technology affected their ability to pass a course. DHS cannot determine if a student’s learning disability should grant them additional time to finish a degree. This job has been and should remain in the hands of the academic institution. This rule would impose additional and unnecessary hurdles for university advisors, DSOs, international students, and, frankly, an already backlogged DHS.

It needs to also be noted it is increasingly taking both domestic and international students longer to complete a bachelor’s than it has in the past. This is due to students encountering financial hardships, changing majors, or taking time off for physical or mental health. When it comes to ESL programs in particular, mandating that 24 months is the amount of time that all students should be given to reach their English language goals is arbitrary and short-sighted. From my time as a language teacher, I know that students can start an English language program at various stages of fluency and practical ability. We need to be very careful about turning away students who bring with them a range of skill sets and perspectives that our academic institutions and companies need just because they may require a little more time to sharpen aspects of their communication skills.

The positive effects of this proposed rule on our campuses and communities are unclear, but the negative consequences would be apparent and dire. Please rescind this rule and allow our students to continue to live, work, and contribute to our country within the strict systems already in place. If students are prevented from coming here and encouraged to pursue their studies elsewhere, they will. The world of the future—full of technological advances, groundbreaking art, scientific discoveries, innovative businesses, and global problem-solving—may very well leave the US behind.

Sincerely,
XXXXX

The proposed rule to eliminate the duration of status for F-1 students represents a fundamental and damaging shift in the United States' long-standing approach to international education. This change will create unnecessary bureaucratic hurdles, stifle academic freedom, and ultimately diminish the global competitiveness of American universities. The current system of duration of status has effectively balanced immigration control with the flexible needs of academic and research pursuits. Replacing it with a rigid, fixed-term visa system ignores the unpredictable nature of graduate research, academic exploration, and the path to degree completion, which can vary due to complex research developments, advisor availability, and the natural progression of intellectual discovery.

The administrative burden this rule places on both students and schools will be immense and counterproductive. Requiring frequent, costly, and time-consuming extension applications will cause significant anxiety for students and create a perpetual fear of losing status due to bureaucratic delays beyond their control. This constant uncertainty will force students to make academic decisions based on immigration paperwork deadlines rather than intellectual curiosity or research requirements. It will inevitably discourage the brightest global minds from choosing the U.S., pushing them toward competitor nations like Canada, the U.K., and Australia, which offer more stable and welcoming academic environments. The loss of this talent will directly harm American innovation, research output, and economic growth.

Furthermore, the rule fails to account for the crucial post-completion Optional Practical Training (OPT) period. OPT is not merely employment; it is an integral extension of the educational experience, allowing students to apply their knowledge in a practical setting. Placing an arbitrary time limit on the initial visa that may not align with a student's program length, plus their authorized OPT period, creates an entirely avoidable point of failure. The potential for a student to have their OPT automatically invalidated because their visa expires before their EAD card does is an unacceptable flaw that will disrupt lives and U.S. employer operations. The current duration of the status model avoids this problem entirely and should be retained. For these reasons, the proposed rule should be withdrawn in its entirety to protect the continued success and preeminence of America’s higher education system and its invaluable contributions to our society and economy.

The filing fee for Form I-539 is currently $470, and while biometrics fees are now included, additional expenses such as legal assistance or premium processing (which costs up to $1,965 for a 30-day turnaround) could easily push the total cost toward $800 or more per application. Consider a student who enters on an F-1 visa for a bachelor's degree but then decides to pursue a master's program upon completion. Under the proposed fixed limits, they would need to apply for an extension well in advance, but with processing times often exceeding a year, they might face a gap in status where they cannot legally study or work. I am writing to express my strong concerns regarding the proposed policy changes to the duration of status for F-1 and J visa holders. The policy appears to be premised on assumptions that are neither proportionate nor supported by the evidence presented.

First, as many have already noted, Ph.D. programs typically require at least five to seven years to complete. Even in the Department’s own materials, the cited “problem cases” do not justify a sweeping change: the document references just over 2,100 individuals who entered the United States between 2000 and 2010 and who would still hold F-1 status in 2025. By the Department’s own account, more than 1.6 million individuals entered in F-1 status in 2023 alone, not counting other years. Even if we were to assume—contrary to fact—that all 2,100 cases constitute abuse of the system, and even if we compare them only to the 2023 cohort, the proportion would be approximately 0.13%. It is neither reasonable nor efficient to overhaul policy in a way that burdens and disrupts millions of law-abiding students every year to address a fraction of a percent of cases.

Second, the document cites several instances of intellectual property theft by individuals holding J visas and then attempts to link these cases to shortening lawful periods of stay for F/J categories. This framing encourages suspicion of foreign nationals rather than addressing the specific security issues at hand. If national security is the true concern, the appropriate remedy is to strengthen background and security vetting in sensitive fields. The materials do not demonstrate that shortening lawful stay periods would prevent intellectual property theft; there is no causal relationship established. Conflating these distinct issues risks spreading fear and xenophobia while aligning with populist impulses, rather than advancing targeted, evidence-based policy.

For these reasons, I respectfully urge the Department to reconsider the proposed changes. A measured approach—focused on rigorous screening in sensitive areas and robust enforcement against genuine abuse—would better protect national interests without imposing unnecessary costs on the vast majority of students who comply fully with U.S. laws and who contribute substantially to our academic and research communities.

As a tax consultant who regularly advises multinational businesses and individuals navigating U.S. tax compliance, I want to highlight why the DHS proposal outlined in the Federal Register (pp. 142–144) presents significant risks.

Thirty days is insufficient for filing final state and federal returns, closing payroll accounts, or managing tax residency issues. This abrupt timeline will result in noncompliance not because of negligence but because of unrealistic deadlines.

Second, forcing students to file multiple extensions of stay (EOS) mirrors what we in tax call unnecessary filing complexity. Each EOS triggers additional forms, biometric fees, and waiting periods. Third, the proposed rule ignores cross-field educational mobility, which is critical for tax and accounting. Many students complete a first degree in general business and later pursue a master’s in taxation or data analytics to meet the 150-credit-hour CPA requirement. Denying the possibility of a second master’s undercuts professional licensure pipelines at a time when the U.S. is already facing a CPA shortage (see AICPA’s pipeline reports, p. 150).

Recommendation: DHS should revise the rule by (1) restoring the 60-day grace period, (2) maintaining Duration of Status (D/S) to align with the inherently variable nature of academic programs, and (3) explicitly permitting students to pursue second master’s degrees in related or STEM-adjacent fields to meet professional licensure requirements. These revisions would protect not just students but the integrity of U.S. tax and compliance systems.

Allowing continuous second-degree enrollment ensures that students remain in the system without interruption, guaranteeing stable cash flow for schools. Every additional degree pursued translates into more semesters of tuition and fees paid to U.S. institutions, which are already navigating financial pressures and declining domestic enrollment. Institutions already have advising systems, libraries, and facilities in place; keeping students enrolled longer allows schools to maximize the return on these investments. Instead of constantly seeking to replace departing students, universities can retain committed learners, spread out fixed costs, and improve long-term planning. The ripple effects go beyond finances—retained students often contribute to research, serve as teaching assistants, and participate in local communities, strengthening both campuses and the towns around them.

For these reasons, restricting second-degree opportunities is not only unnecessary but also harmful to the financial health of U.S. higher education. International students already pay higher tuition rates and receive fewer subsidies than domestic students. Denying them the ability to invest further in U.S. education is a direct blow to both institutions and the broader economy. This policy should be rejected in favor of one that recognizes the economic and academic value international students bring when they are allowed to pursue second degrees without interruption.
